# CityBuilderSim

*Build 0.7.3 · Save format 27 · 22 September 2026*

A macroeconomic city simulator: an age pyramid that decides the workforce, a labour market that prices it, fifteen private sectors on one template trading real goods on real markets — two of them selling to the world, one of them to the mills, one hauling the others' freight and one building the cars the households drive — a share register and an exchange where the bank is the dealer, a bank that cannot lend below what its own money costs it, a central bank whose balance sheet is the only place money is made and whose dial is the price of it, households that each keep their own books including the people the books used to leave out, illness that kills, crime that has reasons, households that eat thirteen separate foods and choose between them by income, own cars and borrow for them, and spend what is left over a counter, a road that carries three kinds of traffic and can be relieved but never deleted, a trade band that is three quarters freight, and a currency with a balance of payments behind it, a vault that spends to defend it and a real rate that moves it. This is what it currently has and does.

## 1. The month

*Everything in the game happens in this order, and most of the hard bugs in its history have been a line that made it into one phase and not the other. The order is genuinely a sequence, so it is numbered — and since 18 September it is also generated: `docs/month-order.md` lists every top-level statement of `Game.nextMonth()` and `SimulationEngine.simulateMonth()` with its line, which is what this list is struck against.*

1. **The central bank settles with the treasury, and the promises are paid** — Before anything is priced. With the autopilot on, the Taylor rule takes the dial. Then the treasury pays the interest on last month's advances, takes last month's profit back as the remittance, repays its central bank out of any cash above zero, pays down arrears, and is advanced whatever it is still short (`settleTreasury()`). Then the holdings dial trades the city's term paper toward its target (`openMarketOperation()`), so this month's quotes carry it. Then the students' grant and EI are paid on the people the month opens with, in the month they are credited, and the bank pays its profit tax.
2. **The world turns and the land office re-prices** — World prices advance, the exchange rate is taken, the cost of living goes into the labour market. What the city pays outside and what businesses pay inside are both inputs to everything below.
3. **Business credit is priced, interest billed, property tax charged** — The bank prices the money first — its premium and its cost of funds — and a failed bank lends nothing. Before the statements run, so the figures each sector banks are net of it.
4. **Every building pays to stand, and every shipper pays its freight** — 1% of build cost a year, charged to every owner in cash *and* materials *and* construction points — placed as a real order with the builders, not a line item. A forty-year stock at 1% a year is about 40% of the city's whole construction output. Then the railway's invoice on the month's trade, for the same reason: an expense on fourteen sets of books and revenue on the fifteenth.
5. **Fifteen income statements are struck** — Retail, real estate, industry, construction, heavy industry, mining, materials, business services, manufacturing, agriculture, food processing, rail, automotive, luxury retail, restaurants — each at the *utilisation the month was traded at*, not at today's, and each from the same template. The VAT is settled from the same figures between the two halves.
6. **National accounts, then the household books** — Household spending *is* consumption, read from the other end, so the people cannot be shown paying a figure the shops were not shown receiving. Consumption is three counters now — the grocers', the boutiques' and the kitchens' — plus the rent.
7. **The households buy cars, then spend the rest over a counter** — With the month's money fresh and before the investor can see it: the second-hand market clears first, because nobody pays forty for a car they can have for twelve, then the showroom; then the boutiques, and the kitchens right after, because they are the same kind of purchase out of the same surplus. The cars, the pieces and the meals count as demand for next month's strike.
8. **The private sector takes its turn** — Loans advance and matured principal comes back; then each sector forecasts its own signal six months out and funds what it plans in a fixed order: sell shares, spend the till, call money home from abroad, and only then borrow.
9. **Construction advances; roads recount; the posts are counted and the labour market reprices** — Sites take the month's points, buy the material that work drew on, and the builders recognise revenue on the same figure the sites advanced by. A shop that opens this morning trades this month and puts its trucks on the road this month — roads are recounted before anything reads them. Then the posts are recounted and wages walk toward what scarcity says per band, and per licence, against this month's posts and before anybody ages.
10. **Demographics** — Age; give birth; die of three separate causes — the band's own rate, illness, and violence; migrate; rebuild the households against last month's; commit and record this month's crime; settle health, education, the police and the transit fare; advance the ring of the sick.
11. **The economy and the services sync** — Population, wages, jobs, the fill rate and the utilisation ratios reach every sector — the road ratio per sector, because only a tram can make two businesses on the same street face different jams, and the health ratio the demographics step has just set.
12. **Cash moves, every market clears, ore is lifted, the paper is paid, the government's books are re-struck** — The utility books what its customers were charged; every market clears and every maker produces in one pass; the mines ask the ground. The paper sold between the presses settles to its holders, the households taking their share first, and the month's coupons and principal are paid holder by holder. The books are re-struck at the bottom of the month, against the same period's spending and after the coupon is known, because the start-of-month call mixed two months' tax fields.
13. **The bank settles, the owners are paid, the shares trade** — The bank pays for whatever paper the households did not take and earns a month of the discount on what it holds; then lending, repayments, interest, deposit rate, branches, the carry trade, the window and the interest on its reserves at the central bank, resolution if it failed, and the cost of funds struck once and final — then the central bank strikes its month's profit, the savers are paid, then dividends, then the exchange, then whatever is still idle goes abroad, the households' by the same rule as the sectors', and a household whose paper no longer out-yields its deposits sells a little of it back to the desk.
14. **The currency moves, and the money is counted** — `MoneyAudit` strikes *pooled after − pooled before = inflows − outflows* across every pool in the city and every flow across its border. A cent of residual is a finding. The hot money moves just before the strike, because it moves a pool; then the balance of payments, the currency and the price index, each reading a month that has finished settling. The currency reads the real rate against the world's, and on a month it is pushed weaker on a deficit the central bank sells the vault's dollars against the push — a capital transaction booked after the audit, because no pool moves on it. Nothing after the audit may move a pool. Every twelfth month autosaves, also before any skip and on quit.

**What moved since the last edition.** The top of the month is new: the treasury settles with its central bank before anything is priced, because the advances and the remittance are money made and destroyed and have to fall inside the audit's window, and the holdings dial trades after that settle and before the market is priced so that this month's quotes carry what it did (0.7.0, 0.7.1). The students' grant (0.7.1) and EI (0.7.3) are paid at the top of the month, on the people the month opens with; for as long as either had existed the households were credited last month's bill while the treasury paid this month's, and nothing saw it because the households are outside the audit's pools. The defence sells dollars inside the currency step (0.7.2). And the construction retainer — set, saved, reset and reformed, and paid by no line of the month — is gone (0.7.1); the standing policy is the lever.

> **Standing rule**
>
> A flow cannot be reconstructed from the state a month ended in. That is why the save carries income statements, the VAT ledger, the inventory baseline in units, wage history, loss streaks, plots consumed, the unburied backlog, last month's household shapes, the ring of the long sick, six months of prisoners, the railway's quote and what it carried, every sector's fleet and the memory of the commute, the treasury's journal for the month that ended and the one in progress, and what the vault sold defending the currency — none of them derivable by looking at the city.

## 2. People

*The age pyramid* is *the population. It used to be a display beside a formula; now nothing else decides how many people live here — and since the long sick and the crime batch, nothing dies of only one thing.*

### Six ages, three ways to die

*The band's own annual mortality. Monthly rates are compounded, not divided by twelve.*

| Band | Ages | Annual mortality | Note |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| Babies | 0–5 | 0.10% | almost all of it in the first year |
| Children | 6–12 | 0.0075% | the safest band there is |
| Teens | 13–17 | 0.02% | accidents |
| Adults | 18–69 | 0.225% | averaged over a fifty-two year span — and the entire workforce |
| Seniors | 70–84 | 2.90% | population-weighted from a life table |
| Elders | 85–119 | 12.77% | plus ageing out at 120 |

**The seniors were one band of fifty years until save format 27**, at a flat 4.5%. Senior care asks for a place for everybody over seventy, and in the real world about one in nine of them is in one — 2% of seventy-four-year-olds against 29.6% of the over-85s — and one band cannot hold a fifteenfold gradient, nor a mortality curve that runs from 1.4% a year at seventy to over 30% at ninety-five. The two figures are population-weighted from Canada's 2019 life table, and the split is very nearly aggregate-preserving: total deaths among the over-seventies went from 6.5% a year to about 6.7%, and a seventy-year-old has 14.9 years left against the 15.4 the single band gave. The over-85s keep two household shapes of their own, because *Elder living alone* is the cell in trouble first when senior care is short.

Children, teens and adults were halved when illness started killing people, so that the new cause of death would be a redistribution rather than a surcharge. A month's deaths are now struck from three rates against the same opening balance — the band's own rate (scaled by care, and by who has no home), **illness** from the ring of the long sick, and **violence** from the month's homicides — capped together at 5% a month, with the cap scaling each part alike so the shares survive it. Every one of them is recorded by band, so the Reports tab can say what the city has died of since it was founded.

Bands drain exponentially rather than on a fixed schedule, so a baby boom smears into a bulge rather than travelling through the city as a wave. Nobody is tracked individually; the bucket only has a mean.

### Migration

The city moves toward a target rather than snapping to one. Housing and jobs say how *attractive* the city is, not how many people are in it.

```
target = (0.75 × jobs × residentsPerJob + 0.25 × housingCapacity) × seniorCarePull
residentsPerJob = (1 + 0.125) / adultShare        // 12.5% labour slack
arrivals   = max(0, target − population) × 0.15 × crowding × crimePull
departures = population × decliningPressure × 0.05
```

Gross flows, not net, so the screen can say *why* the number moved. Crowding interpolates to zero between comfortable households and the point where every flatshare and doubled-up home has already formed — a full city still takes arrivals, just fewer. Nobody leaves unless a pay tier's *real* pay has been declining **twelve months straight** or has stopped entirely. Four more pushes: a band whose wage is pinned at the minimum and still has more workers than posts sheds 2% of the surplus a month, bankrupt households leave, rent above the target burden deters arrivals, and **crime deters arrivals** — calibrated off Cullen & Levitt (1999), a tenth of the city's draw gone at twice Canada's crime rate, almost all of it as people not coming rather than people leaving. Arrivals carry a skill mix drawn from a world with far more labourers than graduates, weighted by the premium each band is paid here.

### Households, pay, and what they remember

**Fifteen household shapes**, from `SENIOR_ALONE` and the over-85s' `ELDER_ALONE` through `COUPLE_TWO_CHILDREN` to `SHARED_ADULTS`. Families are built from the adults who *work*; everyone else has their own books. The mix follows the age pyramid and the job tiers; when homes run short, singles form flatshares first and families double up last.

**The households remember.** The builder keeps last month's households as far as the people still exist for them — 1% of them re-form each month by design — shrinking each shape by the worst shortage among the bands it needs, rebuilding only the remainder, and refitting tiers to the jobs by iterative proportional fitting. Before it, a city redrew every family from scratch every month and wallets moved with the redraw. Eight seeds: orphans at the end **490–633 → 11–19**, hunger **4% → 0%**, unemployment **14.8% → 12.2%**. Everything a cell holds moves with the people when the shapes re-form — savings, debt, shares, the dollars abroad, the student loan, and since 16 September the cars — and the move is clamped so that a pool cannot hand out more than it holds, because the day it could, four retired cells owed minus 2.7e-29 dollars and the *sign* of that decided the exchange rate (see [how it's checked](#20-how-its-checked)).

**Homes have sizes.** A studio takes two, a low-rise flat four, a house six; a household has to fit, largest families into the smallest unit that fits, and a one- or two-person flat refuses a dependant outright. **Rent is two markets** — see [prices](#14-prices-the-currency--the-world). An empty home now costs its owner something to hold, and so does a full one: every building pays 1% of its cost a year to stand.

*Six pay tiers, eleven job types — base wages on NS Job Bank medians*

| Tier | Monthly |
| --- | ---: |
| Unskilled | $3,460 |
| Skilled | $4,500 |
| College | $5,500 |
| Professional | $8,200 |
| Senior professional | $9,600 |
| Elite | $15,600 |

> **Seventy-eight ledgers**
>
> Eleven working shapes × six pay tiers, four retired rows, three kinds of out-of-work, students, orphans by age band, and the prisoners. Each keeps savings, debt, a lockout clock, shares in each of the sixteen listed companies, dollars held abroad, student debt, its cars, the month's investment income, the dinners it ate out, the share of its people who could pay for care and the city's own paper — thirty-one slots a cell in the save, each keyed by name so a new row never shifts an old one, and each new slot appended to the end so that an older save reads as a city that had none of it, which it did not.
>
> Since 0.7.2 a cell whose census count falls under half a household (`HouseholdBalance.EMPTY_CELL`) is empty: it keeps its count, holds nothing and is paid nothing, and every stock it held folds to its own row first and then to the city — because a cell of 1e-15 households was still being paid, and one line divided a credit by it.

### The household books, and a balance sheet

Every cell shows wages, the banded wage tax, pension contributions and pensions, the health premium, rent, tuition, interest, shopping, healthcare fees, the transit fare, and what is left — plus **savings, debt, shares, the city's paper and cars per household**, and a waterfall: payslip, rent, fees, food; short, and they spend savings, then sell the city's paper back to the bank's desk, then bring their paper home from abroad, then sell shares at the bid, then borrow from the bank at the city's rate plus a spread that climbs with what they already owe, and only then eat less — which makes them ill. A row six months of income in debt that still cannot cover subsistence **goes bankrupt**: 4% a month discharged, locked out of credit for a year, a quarter of them leaving the city. A row that *can* be evicted and still cannot pay loses the share of its homes the shortfall covers.

Spending follows income, and since 17 September it follows wealth too. A household plans to spend 80% of what is left above subsistence at the grocer's, so shopping is a budget rather than a headcount; on top of that it spends 0.33% of its net worth a month — four percent a year, the middle of the measured propensity to consume out of wealth — and puts half of the income it does not spend on food over a luxury counter and a quarter of it on a table. Dividends and the coupon on its paper abroad are paid home and enter the plan, and so, since 0.7.1, are the coupons on the city's own paper, paid into savings as untaxed investment income. A household with no debt, no lockout and more than three months of disposable income in the bank puts 30% of the excess into shares, and sends the rest of its idle savings abroad on the same rule the sectors use. It also takes the city's paper at issue: at the settle the households go first, taking a fifth of an issue for every point it yields over the deposit rate (`HOUSEHOLD_PAPER_APPETITE`) and never more than half (`MAX_HOUSEHOLD_PAPER_SHARE`), out of savings past the cushion, and the bank buys the rest. Pensions are pay-as-you-go, and both the contribution rate and the replacement rate are Policy dials. Contributions follow workers and pensions follow pensioners, so an ageing city buys a structural deficit without changing a single policy.

**And since 0.7.3 saving answers the real rate.** Everything a household plans above a basket a head — the propensity's share, the wealth term, and the surplus the counter and the table spend out of — is multiplied by one factor a month struck on the real deposit rate, the bank's deposit rate less the year's inflation: ten points of real return cut it by a tenth, ten points of negative real return raise it by a tenth, and it is held between a half and one and a half. Subsistence never moves, and at a factor of one the plan is the old plan to the bit. On the default seed on 22 September savers ended the run earning 3.63% real and the households planned 0.964 of what they would spend above a basket at zero; over 4,005 months the factor ran from 0.835 to 1.131, median 0.993. What it does to prices is almost nothing, and why is in [the central bank](#13-the-central-bank).

> **Why the households were rich**
>
> Household net worth ran at **45 months of the city's GDP at month 480** — dead on the real world's sixty to eighty-four — and **5,072 by month 3,840**. It did not sit at a wrong level; it diverged. Over one run the foreign coupons came to **$2,649bn against $584bn of every wage the city ever paid**, because the households kept about 79% of their wealth abroad at the world's 2% and the coupon was rolled where it was earned, so wealth compounded at 1.58% a year mechanically, 193× over 333 years. Three changes were ensembled one at a time: paying the coupon home took the ratio from 5,380 months to 3,412; letting investment income into the plan put it back to **5,465**, because investment income is a *flow* and a bigger city pays more of it; the wealth term took it to 2,737 and gave the best city of the four. *A stock that compounds can only be bounded by a drain that reads the stock.* And with the coefficient pushed to nine times the empirical range the stock still rose, while delivery fell from 76% of plans to 57% — the households are not hoarding because they are misers; they are hoarding because there is nothing to buy. The cars, the boutiques and the kitchens are the answer to that, and net worth now oscillates (432 → 137 → 128 → 214 months of GDP) instead of climbing.

### What a household owns, and borrows for

**A car is a household stock**, beside savings, debt, shares and the dollars abroad — it follows the people, it is saved per cell by name, a household that leaves takes it — and it is the first one that is *not money*, so a currency reform does not touch it. It is the first durable a household in this game has ever been able to own: the measurement that decided the shape found an unskilled couple banking \$3,160 of a \$4,880 month and sitting on **\$799,100, a hundred and sixty-four months of income**, with \$17.6bn of household savings in the city against zero household debt. That is not a rich city, it is a city with nothing to buy. So affordability barely binds in a mature city and binds hard in a young one, and the constraint is time: 2% of the households that have never owned one buy a car in a month, a car lasts 180 months and is replaced at once when it dies, one per household is saturation, and a cell buys *whole* cars — because a money ratio that comes out as a physical quantity has to cross at a grain coarser than the dust, or a reformed city wants an ulp more of a car and the two cities' trade balances part company. A city whose transit could carry everybody tops out at **half a car per household, for ever**; a metro built after the cars does not remove them, it stops them being replaced, and the fleet decays to the new ceiling over the life of a car.

**And they borrow for it.** Jerus: *"make it so that citizens the car requirements are lowered and instead they finance with the bank."* The rule is *pay what you have and borrow the difference*: a household hands over every dollar it has spare and a lender finds the rest, with a fifth of the price (`CAR_DEPOSIT`) as a minimum in cash and half the household's remaining credit room as the most a lender advances — that second number found by `DenominationCheck`, because every financed household was parked within a whisker of the bankruptcy line. With no credit line the rule reduces exactly to the old cash rule, so it can never refuse a purchase the old one allowed. The first draft — a fifth down, four fifths borrowed, compulsory — cut ownership at month 266 from 42% to 11%, because these households are cash-rich and income-poor and the loan moved the constraint onto the thing they have not. Seven of eight seeds are bit-identical over four thousand months; the young city diverges in month eight and has bought twice the cars by month ten. The loan is a bridge, not a note: the grocery waterfall repays it out of spare cash within a month or two. Household debt in this game had been exactly zero in every measured city. It is not any more.

**The car goes last.** Jerus: *"if they are doing bad they cut back expenses, sell their cars or go for cheaper groceries."* Two of the three were already in — the plan shrinks by itself, and a poorer cell already buys more grain and less meat — and the car was in nothing: a family sold its shares, brought its paper home, drew its last dollar of credit and went hungry with five months of take-home parked in the drive. There is a **second-hand market at home** now, and the fleet does not shrink when a household sells, it changes hands. The price is struck the way every market here strikes one: a floor at 15% of new (what a scrapper pays), a ceiling at 70%, a position between them from demand against supply — so a city cannot sell its way out of a general crash: everybody offers, nobody buys, the price is scrap, and the harness asserts it (8,000 offered, 0 sold, pinned at the floor). A household offers when the wage after the fixed bills no longer buys the food *and* half a year of that gap beats everything it has saved and can still borrow; a one-month test found households going bankrupt with the car still in the drive thirteen times for every one that sold it. Over 4,002 months of the default run when it shipped the trigger fired in two cell-months, both fractions of a household, and over 4,005 on 22 September in none, because the households were too rich to ever sell anything — which is the finding above, and the reason the counter and the kitchens exist.

## 3. Outside the families

*Until this system the city's money was spread across every adult in a pay tier, working or not, so an unskilled single adult took home $1,262 in a month of 40% unemployment and nobody was ever poor. Four groups now keep their own books beside the families.*

```
labour force  = workforce − students − prisoners
the pool      = labour force − filled posts        // an identity, not a second count
```

| Row | Lives on | What is true of them |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On EI | 55% of the wage they lost, capped | a claim runs twelve months; the benefit is split among claimants out of a real premium |
| EI run out | savings, then credit | the only row that can be evicted; four in five of the pool end up here |
| Lost their home | nothing | hungry, and **3.7×** as likely to be ill and to die |
| Students | savings, a grant, and a loan, interest-free unless the player sets a rate | out of the labour supply until they graduate; graduates repay over 114 months |
| Orphans | nothing, and they pay no fees | one row per age band; no grown-up, so no credit |
| Prisoners | nothing; debts frozen | out of the labour force, out of the housing match, out of every offender group |

**Employment insurance is a real programme.** A 1.63% premium off insurable wages funds a 55% benefit capped at Canada's maximum insurable earnings scaled to the city's unskilled median — $1,903 a month for an unskilled claimant, $3,158 for anyone at or above the cap. Both rates are Policy dials. The ring is struck on the *inflow* of the newly unemployed, cohort by cohort: jobs lost this month join at the wage they lost, each cohort is thinned monthly by hires, deaths and departures, and the twelfth cohort falls off the end into "EI run out". Arrivals who never found work enter at the unskilled wage and get no claim. Since 0.7.3 the benefit is paid in the month it is credited: struck again at the top of the month on the pool the month opens with and paid there (`Game.payEiBenefits()`), so the treasury, the ledger and the audit read one figure. For as long as EI had existed the out of work were credited last month's bill while the treasury paid this month's, and nothing saw it because the households are outside the audit's pools; `OutsideCheck` closes every Construction Depot in a small city and asserts that the closing month pays the EI of the pool it opened with and the month after pays the bill the closing struck, each credited the month it is paid; three of its lines fail on the old order. A save from 0.7.2 pays one month's EI twice on its first month, once.

**Eviction is a level, not a rate.** A row that can be evicted and is short loses `households × min(1, shortfall / (rent + fees + interest))` of its homes; a quarter of those leave the city and the rest are on the street. Because a cell is an average, its households run out together — evictions arrive as a cliff. For most of the project's life nobody was ever evicted in the ensemble: an out-of-work adult ended a 333-year run holding millions, because the unskilled tier's savings are what they draw on first. It moves with the run. On the default seed on 18 September, with the wealth term and the counters in, 550 households were evicted over 4,002 months and 137 of them left; on 22 September, at 0.7.3, nobody was evicted over 4,005 months, nobody was left on EI at the end, and an out-of-work adult whose claim had run out ended the run with $303,200 put by. Close the biggest employer in a young city and the path works exactly as designed: **549 evicted in the first year, 440 of them in two months, 384 on the street at the worst, 127 still there four years later** (measured on 11 September; no harness reproduces it since).

Housing serves each group with its own valve: an out-of-work adult alone counts a full door, a flatsharer a fifth, a doubled-up seeker or someone on the street none — so the rent bill is split over the doors actually paid for. The transit fare is a third fee beside the health fee and the tuition, split across the rows the way the clinic's fees are: from the day transit was built until 16 September it was credited to the city and debited to nobody, and nobody saw it because no fixture had ever built a bus — see [transport](#18-transport--vehicles).

## 4. Health

*Three classes. `Health` is the effect — a multiplier on output. `Healthcare` is the service — an employer with a payroll and a cemetery with a finite number of plots. `Sickness` is the ring of people who have not got better, and it is the one that kills.*

### Sickness is the fourth utilisation ratio

It sits beside energy, water and roads — and, since 17 September, beside the fifth ratio, the sector's own fleet of vans — multiplies with them, and is carried across a save the same way. The one difference is the whole point:

```
output  = capacity × fill × bEnergy × bWater × bRoad × bHealth × bVans
payroll = wages × fill                          // no bHealth, no ratio at all
```

Output falls, payroll does not. **The employer carries it** — a mill with fifty on the books pays fifty wages in a bad flu month and sells four weeks of output in three. The workforce, the pyramid and the wage bill never move. A sick worker still gets paid, still shops, still pays rent.

*General-care coverage sets the standing absence rate*

| Coverage | Off sick |
| --- | ---: |
| None | 18.0% |
| Half | 10.5% |
| Everybody | 3.0% |

Five things add on top of that baseline and the total is capped at 45%: an outbreak, the unburied (up to 15 points), hunger (up to 8), the share of the city with no home at 3.7 times the baseline, and **the injured** — half a month off work for every violent crime.

**Outbreaks** land on top: roughly one every five years, peaking 8–25%, decaying 55% a month, with hospitals taking 60% off the peak but never preventing one. The roll is a pure function of the month number, so an epidemic survives a reload without the generator's state going in the save — you cannot save-scum out of one. Measured over 4,005 months on the default seed, 22 September: **52 outbreaks, the city ill for 289 months, worst month 45%** — which is the cap; and the run ends at 15.1% with no outbreak in it at all, nobody unburied and two points of hunger on a baseline of 12.8% that general care covered 35% of. On 18 September the same seed ended at 36.8%, fifteen points of it the unburied; the batches since moved every seed, so the two readings are two cities, not a trend.

### The people who stay sick

Each band carries a thirteen-month ring of who fell ill when. Past **two months** sick, a share of them dies each month — 4% for babies and seniors, 8% for the over-85s, 2% for adults, 1% for children and teens. General care is what gets people out of the ring: it cures 50% of the sick a month untreated and 90% fully served. Babies and the retired fall ill twice as often as the city rate until their own care takes the excess away.

> **What general care stopped doing**
>
> It used to be a ×3 swing on the death rate of every teen and adult. That is gone: general care now acts *only* through the sick rate and through curing the sick. A fully served adult used to die at 0.15% a year; they now die at about 0.232%, base plus a sliver of illness. The halving of the base rate does not make that back at the good end — deliberately, and it is a live lever.

### What care does to a life

A multiplier on the band's annual death rate, interpolated *geometrically* on coverage — unserved is multiplied by the swing, fully served is divided by it, half-served is exactly the base rate. Log space is the right space for a multiplier: halfway between "forty times worse" and "forty times better" is *the same*.

*Annual mortality all-in: the band's rate scaled by care, plus steady-state illness — struck before the seniors were split at 85, and kept as it was struck; the two bands now start from 2.90% and 12.77%, with swings of 1.35× and 1.80×*

| Band | Care type | Swing | No care | Half | Full |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Babies | Childcare | 40× | 7.96% | 0.77% | 0.017% |
| Children | Childcare | 40× | 0.83% | 0.120% | 0.004% |
| Teens | General | — | 0.56% | 0.133% | 0.024% |
| Adults | General | — | 1.28% | 0.449% | 0.232% |
| Seniors | Senior | 1.35× | 9.96% | 5.14% | 3.35% |

Teens and adults have no swing left; the whole of their column is illness. Senior care's swing is 1.35× on the 70-to-85 band and 1.80× on the over-85s, because that is where the care is worth more. Childcare also **doubles the birth rate** at full coverage — 15 per thousand a year to 30 — and senior care makes the city **30% more attractive** to migrants, which is what turns an ageing pyramid into something to manage rather than endure.

Measured on the default seed on 22 September: **illness is 32.7% of all deaths** — 147,312 of 450,113 over 4,005 months, against 42.7% on 18 September. Two editions ago the same figure read 1.4%, 655 of 46,134, and that difference is not the model: until 17 September the hunger measure was reporting zero in a city that was starving, and the sick rate it feeds was being fed a zero (see [what a household eats](#7-goods--markets)); and the playtest's default player leaves the city alone for fifty-four months at a stretch, so every figure it reports is a city in crisis from neglect. A player who tops up power, water, streets, clinics and stores once a year runs the same seeds at 7.8% sick against 23.1%. Babies take the worst of it: twice as often ill, 4% a month past two months, on top of childcare's ×40.

### The two ways to bury somebody

A cemetery is a *stock*: plots are consumed permanently and the land never comes back. A crematorium is a *rate*: almost no land, a great deal of electricity, breaking even only when busy. Households whose monthly surplus would cover a plot over ten years choose burial; the rest choose cremation; overflow runs both ways. A city with neither leaves people where they fell, and **the unburied make the living ill** — up to 15 points on the sick rate, cleared the month a cemetery opens.

### Somebody pays for all of it

Healthcare carries **2,128 jobs** across its fourteen templates, more than any other category the city pays for — only the railway's three offer more. The treasury pays the staffed payroll plus maintenance, less what patients and funerals bring back — measured at about **20% cost recovery** when the ring was added, and 25% on the default seed on 22 September, $5.04M a month, with 246 buried and none cremated in the last month of the run: a net-deficit business at the founding fees, as designed, and since 0.6.8 the player's to make something else. Fees are charged on people *served*, not beds built, so an empty ward is paid for and collects nothing — and since 0.6.8 served means treated.

*Same 600-house city, 360 months, four programmes — measured before the base rates were halved and the sick ring added, and kept because the* shape *is what it is for*

| Programme | Population | Off sick | Births/mo | GDP/mo |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Nothing | 1,232 | 33.0% | 1.5 | $693k |
| General + death care | 1,496 | 3.0% | 1.9 | $1,298k |
| … plus childcare | 2,813 | 3.0% | 5.6 | $2,214k |
| Everything | 4,461 | 3.0% | 7.9 | $3,305k |

The city is founded with a doctor, a nursery, an almshouse, a churchyard and a constabulary — enough for about 1,200 people, sized off the pyramid's own equilibrium shares, and not a building among them. The churchyard's graves last four centuries for a village and six years for a city of eighty thousand.

### The price at the door

Jerus: *"healthcare should be an adjustable price, all the way to even make it a profitable business or the option to make it an obligatory insurance payment system."* Two dials since 0.6.8. `TaxPolicy.healthFeeScale` multiplies the three care fees — general, childcare and senior; funerals are deliberately unscaled — from nothing to 15× the founding ones, and `healthPremiumRate` takes up to 10% of every wage, employee side, on the EI premium's own base, into the treasury with nothing balancing it. Between them the Policy tab's *Promises → Health* page names three corners: free at the point of use and paid from taxes; a business, fees past the city's own break-even, which the page strikes live (`Healthcare.breakEvenScale()`, the gross cost over what the fees would raise at 1×); or insurance, no fee and a premium. The ceiling went from 5 to 15 after the first measurement, because a played city breaks even at ×7 to ×13 — the founding fees were set against founding wages, and the labour market has lifted a clinic's payroll since. The default seed on 22 September breaks even at ×9.85.

**A household that cannot pay goes without care, not without food** — Jerus's rule, and what makes the fee a decision. The share of a household's bill that fits in what its plan says it will have after rent, its other bills and a basket for everybody in it — counting income, savings, the paper abroad and the credit still open, the waterfall's own order — is the share of its people the clinics treat, struck against the bill at full service so that a household that skipped last month does not read an empty bill as affordable and swing between served and starving. The rest go untreated in the sick rate, the swings and the births. A household that can cover its bills is served exactly as before, multiplied by exactly 1.0 and asserted at zero tolerance, so at the founding fee the cliff catches only households with nothing, the out of work past EI and elders on a pension: 0 to 247 people a month across the eight seeds, and none on the default seed on 22 September. Fees at ×5 recovered about two thirds of the cost and priced out no more people than ×1, because the households the cliff catches are out at any positive fee and the working poor can still find $50 a head — a fee that prices a family out of childcare is a fee the dial cannot yet set. `HealthCheck`'s sections 12–16 walk it: the scale against the constants, the break-even, one household both ways, a poor city three times, a rich one at zero tolerance, and the premium to the penny.

## 5. Crime & police

*Crime has reasons. Every adult at liberty is sorted once a month, cell by cell, into a graded list of them — because the cells are the only place the reasons meet: the pool knows who is out of work, the housing match knows who has no door and who is crowded, and the household books know who is going short.*

*The reasons, in order. Where a group overlaps another, the higher weight counts.*

| Reason | Weight |
| --- | ---: |
| No home | 5 |
| Out of work, EI run out | 4 |
| Short of money | 3 |
| Out of work, still on EI | 2 |
| Crowded — doubled up or flatsharing | 2 |
| No reason at all | 0.1 |
| *plus* too few police, per adult | 2 |

```
pressure = Σ adults × weight + 2 × (1 − coverage) × adults
crimes   = K × pressure × (1 − 0.90 × coverage^1.5)
coverage = staffed officers / (360 per 100,000)
```

**K is struck, not typed.** It is solved at startup so that a city with Canada's police coverage and the game's own equilibrium adult share commits Canada's 5,585 crimes per 100,000 a year. Full coverage is twice Canada's 180 officers per 100,000 and takes **90%** off — drastically, and never to nothing, which was the brief.

A quarter of crimes are violent. Each costs its victim **half a month off work**, which goes onto the sick rate as an injury term, and **0.115%** of them kill — calibrated against Canada's 1.61 homicides per 100,000. The rest is theft, worth a quarter of an unskilled monthly wage each, half taken from households and half from the tills, and handed to the offenders in proportion to the weight their own cell carried. Theft leaves a sector's books through a named `stolen` line, so the money identity can see it.

**Arrests scale with coverage**: 9% of crimes at full coverage, pro rata below it. Everyone caught serves six months in a ring of monthly cohorts. A prisoner is out of the labour force, out of the housing match, out of every offender group, has their debts frozen and keeps their own ledger row. **Caught and not held is a real state**: with no cell free, the arrest is recorded and the person walks.

*Four buildings, all paid for by the city like the hospitals and the schools*

| Building | Capacity | Jobs | All-in |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Police Station | 120 officers | 172 | $45M |
| Police Headquarters | 500 officers | 750 | $180M |
| Jail | 300 cells | 264 | $360M |
| Penitentiary | 600 cells | 590 | $600M |

Measured over eight 333-year seeds: crime runs at **1.8–2.3 times Canada's rate** in the years before the first station and settles at **about a tenth of it** once coverage is full, with the residue coming almost entirely from the long-term unemployed and the crowded. Between 2,100 and 2,900 people are caught over a run and *every one of them walks*, because the smallest prison in the catalogue is 300 cells for $360M and a city of 15,000 never needs or affords one. Seven to ten people are killed over three centuries; $12.8M to $18.6M is stolen. Those were cities of fifteen thousand. The default seed on 22 September ends at 130,978 people with three police stations, coverage at 46%, crime at 1.22× Canada's, **59,189 caught over the run and every one of them still walking**, 334 killed and $891M stolen — the advisor builds a station three times in four thousand months and a prison never, so the lockup question below has not gone away, it has grown.

## 6. Work & output

*Fifteen private sectors, each keeping its own books, its own cash reserve, its own debt and its own share register — and, since 11 September, each of them* one class *extending a single template. Eight of the fifteen have been added since, five of them in the three days to 18 September, and the whole point of the template is that each cost an afternoon rather than a week.*

> **Why there is a template**
>
> Jerus: *"we should make a single template, and every single sector just extends it, and adds or overrides, right? cause in the future there will be over a thousand or near a thousand sectors."* Before it, six sectors were five handlers in five shapes, named by hand in about a hundred places — eleven loops in the economy manager, a six-way switch in the books, thirteen enumerations in the interface. A seventh would have been a week of finding them. It is now one class, one constant, one line in the registry. Sixty files changed, fifteen new, eight deleted; save format 21 and a clean break.

Everything a sector has is declared once in the template: its **identity** (a saved key, a label, the build-menu group its buildings sit under), its **buildings** (every template in `buildings.json` names its owner, and the sector reads capacity, jobs, land, book value, power, water and road load off its own stacks), its **production** (what it makes, what it uses, how many months it stocks), its **books** (one statement, one shape), its **credit, listing and money abroad**, its **planning**, and its **save**. A sector class is now a declaration of about twenty lines. Mining is the shortest, and the shape a thousand of them should have.

| Sector | Makes | Uses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retail | groceries, priced cost-plus at the shelf | thirteen foods — local first and imports for the shortfall: bread and bakery goods from the ovens, dairy, eggs, meat, vegetables and fruit from the farms, the five processed goods from the plants; grains and fish only ever off a ship |
| Real estate | housing — one rent cheque per occupied home | houses and apartment blocks from construction |
| Industry | bread and bakery goods | crops from local fields first, imports for the shortfall — it used to make food out of nothing |
| Heavy industry | steel, exported or sold to the fabricators | local ore first, imported scrap for the shortfall |
| Mining | iron ore | a deposit, which the player must buy as land |
| Construction | building work, recognised as it is delivered | materials |
| Materials | construction material | power, water, wages |
| Business services | support, back-office and engineering work, by the seat-month, all of it sold abroad | people, almost entirely — and an engineering office needs licensed engineers before it will open at all |
| Manufacturing | fabricated steel and machinery — export only until 16 September, when the assembly plants became their first customer at home | steel, local or imported — 61% of a fabricator's revenue |
| Agriculture | crops for the mills; and since 16 September dairy and eggs, meat, vegetables and fruit for the shelf and the meat works | land, heavily; labour and power barely |
| Food processing | processed meats, ready meals, snacks, cooking fats, drinks — a third of the shelf by weight | meat, vegetables and grains at the Meat Works, crops at the other two; the first customer the Livestock Farm ever had at home |
| Rail | haulage — the freight that used to leave inside the trade band, billed to the shipper at home as a fraction of the lorry rate | track, wagon sets it buys from the Locomotive Works, and fuel imported from the world |
| Automotive | cars for the households and the world; vans for the sectors and wagon sets for the railway, which the world will not buy | fabricated steel and machinery — the first thing in the city that buys either |
| Luxury retail | a counter: watches sold at a margin struck against the queue at the door | luxury goods, all of them imported, deliberately |
| Restaurants | meals, one ninetieth of a person-month each, at three to eight times what the food cost | the same thirteen foods off the same shelf at the same prices — it imports nothing |

**Materials is the seventh**, and the first sector added under the template. The Construction Materials Plant used to feed the city's yard for free; it is a business now, filling a shed rather than planning to two months of demand, and planning on a thirty-six-month view because a building boom is not a month long. A city that builds hard makes materials dear, and a plant near the builders is the first thing in the game that gets cheaper for the buyer *and* richer for the maker at once.

### The eleventh to the fifteenth

**Food processing is the eleventh.** Jerus: *"now a new sector which makes the ready meals, processed meals, snacks, drinks, and cooking fats?"* Those five are 16.3 kg of the reference basket's 50, a third of what a household eats by weight, and every gram of them arrived by ship. Three plants, each decided by a different number: the Meat Works buys meat, vegetables and grains and makes processed meats and ready meals, with the input bill at 40% of revenue; the Snack & Oils Plant turns crops into snacks and cooking fats at 19%; the Bottling Plant turns crops into drinks at 4%. It took four calibration passes and three of them were not calibration: the generic planner sizes a sector by *one* good and skipped every template that did not make it, so two of the three plants were not refused but invisible; a first plant was valued at the import ceiling its own arrival would end, so processed meat stood at $8.90 the month the works was financed and $7.70 the month it opened, and the sector now prices its own plant with its nameplate in the supply; and the sales tax was not in the estimate, which matters here because an import carries no input credit and a city with no herds imports every gram — month 72 of one run read $35k of revenue, $1k of operating income and $5k of tax.

Then the calibration itself, by revenue per worker, which is the ratio that decides whether a maker survives a city growing up: the first pass ran \$6,000–\$10,700 a head against the two bakeries' \$13,500 and \$17,800 and a foundry's \$33,600, and a Bottling Plant was six people making a tonne a day; the three are \$17,100, \$16,800 and \$18,000 a head now, payroll 21–22% of revenue at mid-band. And one rule no other sector needs: **nobody builds a food plant on exports**, because the world's band is narrower than the processing step — raw meat lands at \$7.00 and processed meat ships at \$5.60 — so a plant is financed only when the city already eats what it would make. What the sector is for, in one measurement: at month 98 of a real city the same Meat Works is worth **\$16,559 a month on meat at a farm's export floor and \$1,678 on meat off a ship**. The building did not change; the farms did. Eight seeds: median GDP up 11%, \$375.8M to \$417.9M a month, population unchanged, the sector ending every seed with \$52M–\$86M of assets and zero write-downs in seven of eight.

**Rail is the twelfth and Automotive the thirteenth**, and both are told in [transport](#18-transport--vehicles): the railway is the business that wants to be paid the freight every price in this game has always had inside it, and the assembly plant is the first thing in the city that buys a beam or a machine — ore, steel, fabrication, and now something a person drives away in.

**Luxury retail is the fourteenth.** Jerus: *"lets add restuarants as well as luxury stores, these two will absorb some spending as well"*, and on the pricing, *"supply v demand, thats the most important thing."* A Boutique and a Department Store import what they sell — the world has no shortage of watches — and what a city can be short of is a counter, so the margin is what gets struck, on the market's own rule with a mark-up in place of a price: 1.25× the landed cost with nobody in the shop, 4.00× with a queue at the door, and the position between them from what is wanted against what the counters can serve. Crowded shops widen the margin, a wide margin makes boutiques worth building, and the investor builds them. What it is for is the hoard: household net worth stops diverging and starts oscillating. It is deliberately an import, so a rich city's spending leaves rather than going round again. It is also a fragile business — on one seed it finishes with 22 write-downs and a 252-month borrowing ban — and the sizing of the two buildings against a city's luxury budget has not been tuned.

**Restaurants are the fifteenth**, and the rule Jerus attached is what makes them a different sector rather than a second boutique: *a meal out replaces groceries*. So a kitchen imports nothing. A dinner is the same thirteen foods off the same shelf at the same prices, which makes the kitchens a **second buyer** in a market the city is already short of — where *"let the basket get dearer, not bigger"* actually bites — and a **second door** to the food there is, since Retail's binding constraint is coverage rather than stock. A meal is one ninetieth of a person-month, three a day for thirty days, and the hunger measure counts a dinner at what a person-month of food costs, not at what the kitchen charged, because three to eight times the food is wages, rent and somebody else's washing up and none of it is nourishment. The margin is 3.0× to 8.0×, wider than the trade's own 2.9–3.6× because in this city labour runs at four times food — three centuries of farms and food plants made food cheap while the wage schedule did not move — and at most a third of anybody's meals are eaten out. The harness caught three faults nothing else would have: the sector had no demand at all, because a share of a rich household's *surplus* is a share of zero once the wealth term is in the plan; the kitchens could not pay their staff, because a building pays at 100% and serves at the operating rate, which is about half; and a kitchen that stocked for what it served last month was self-limiting for ever. Eight seeds against 0.6.6: **median hunger 36% to 22%**, sickness 18.1% to 16.6%, the kitchens feeding 11–26% of each city and the shops selling about 5% fewer baskets, which is the crowding-out working. The sector finishes seven seeds of eight with zero write-downs at 2.00% credit, which is the profile of a business that cannot fail, and that is on the list.

### Five ratios, and they multiply

| Ratio | Short of it because | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Energy | generation below draw | a step: output scales with the share delivered, and the bill scales with it too |
| Water | supply below draw | same shape; residents draw 0.3 units a head and nobody bills them |
| Roads | load past 90% of capacity | non-linear, floored at 35% — a gridlocked city still moves, slowly; per sector since the streams were split, because a tram takes one business's staff out of the jam and leaves the one next door's lorries in it |
| Health | the workforce is ill or hurt | cuts output only; the payroll is paid in full |
| Vans | the sector has not taken delivery of the lorries its plant needs | the only one a business *buys*: a fleet is built up at an eighth a month, wears out over ten years, and a firm with none is slowed to 60%, not stopped — it hires haulage |

On top of those sits the **job fill rate**, worked out per job type: the allocator spends the workforce across the posts the city offers, and a sector's payroll and output are both discounted by how much of its establishment it could actually staff. The four that arrive from outside are the city's to fix; the fifth is the sector's own capital, and is told with the vehicles in [transport](#18-transport--vehicles).

> **Why it is a ratio basis and not a ratio**
>
> A month's income statement is written at the start of the month, off last month's utilisation. The simulation then moves it. Save after that and a reloaded game would price the month at ratios it was never traded at — which showed up the day roads arrived, as $0.51 of income appearing out of a reload. Every statement carries the utilisation it was struck against.

### Maintenance is an operating cost, and it is demand

Every building in the city pays 1% of its build cost a year to stand — every sector, every city-maintained category, and the bank's branches — in cash, in materials *and* in construction points, placed as a real order with the builders rather than written off as a line. On a forty-year stock that is about **40% of the city's whole construction output**, permanently. Charging it made the city *bigger*: population 74,043 → 77,121, GDP $81.7M → $106.2M a month, unemployment 41.5% → 37.6% — because maintenance here is somebody's order book.

Construction recognises revenue *as work is delivered*: an order adds to unearned revenue and a backlog, each month's points earn their share, and the builders buy their material as they build. Booking it all up front made the sector look enormously profitable in a boom and catastrophic the year after. Its payroll has a 25% idle floor — crews cost something even with nothing to build, which is what makes the shedding spiral possible and worth warning about.

## 7. Goods & markets

*There used to be two bespoke markets, one for food and one for iron, each with its own formula and its own bugs. There is one rule now, and thirty-one goods that obey it or opt out — thirteen of which are the food on a grocer's shelf, three of which are vehicles, and two of which the world makes and will not buy back.*

*World prices are in the world's money and reach the city through the exchange rate; the third number is what moving one unit costs, three quarters of the wedge between the other two*

| Good | Unit | Import | Export | Freight | Priced |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Crops | tonne | $440 | $280 | $60 | on the band |
| Grains | kg | $0.80 | $0.50 | $0.11 | on the band |
| Bread | kg | $2.50 | $1.60 | $0.34 | on the band |
| Dairy and eggs | kg | $3.00 | $1.90 | $0.41 | on the band |
| Vegetables | kg | $1.80 | $1.10 | $0.26 | on the band |
| Fruit | kg | $2.50 | $1.50 | $0.38 | on the band |
| Meat | kg | $7.00 | $4.40 | $0.98 | on the band |
| Fish | kg | $8.00 | $5.00 | $1.13 | on the band |
| Cooking fats | kg | $3.00 | $1.90 | $0.41 | on the band |
| Processed meats | kg | $9.00 | $5.60 | $1.28 | on the band |
| Ready meals | kg | $8.00 | $5.00 | $1.13 | on the band |
| Bakery goods | kg | $6.00 | $3.70 | $0.86 | on the band |
| Snacks | kg | $10.00 | $6.20 | $1.43 | on the band |
| Drinks | kg | $1.50 | $0.90 | $0.23 | on the band |
| Iron | tonne | $410 | $140 | $101 | on the band — freight is half of what delivered ore costs |
| Steel | tonne | $1,284 | $847 | $164 | on the band — the ceiling arrived the day something in the city started buying it |
| Materials | unit | $18,000 | $7,200 | $4,050 | on the band |
| Groceries | unit | — | — | — | by the seller (cost-plus) |
| Housing | home | — | — | — | by the seller (the rent market) |
| Building work | point | — | — | — | by the seller |
| Fabricated steel | tonne | — | $2,210 | $486 | on the band, export only — deliberately: the bulky input is the one a city must make itself |
| Machinery | tonne | $14,300 | $9,000 | $1,980 | on the band — its ceiling arrived on 16 September, the day an assembly plant bought one |
| Support work | seat-month | — | $5,500 | — | on the band, export only; nothing to ship |
| Back-office work | seat-month | — | $8,600 | — | on the band, export only |
| Engineering work | seat-month | — | $14,600 | — | on the band, export only |
| Cars | car | $44,000 | $36,000 | $3,000 | on the band — 10% either side of the middle price where the shelf's foods run 21–25%, which is what value density does: moving a car costs about what moving two tonnes of steel costs, and the car is worth thirty-four times as much |
| Vans and trucks | van | $72,000 | — | $4,500 | on the band, and the world will not buy one — with makers and no takers the floor is zero |
| Rolling stock | wagon set | $2,400,000 | — | $150,000 | on the band, and the world will not buy one; the dearest thing it sells the city |
| Luxury goods | piece | $9,000 | — | $350 | on the band, imported and never exported |
| Luxury retail | piece | — | — | — | by the seller: the margin over the landed cost, struck against the queue |
| Restaurant meals | meal | — | — | — | by the seller: the margin over the food, struck against the tables |

```
supply   = flow + stock / 6              // never the raw stockpile
position = demand / (demand + supply)
price    = exportPrice + (importPrice − exportPrice) × position
```

The symmetric form is load-bearing. `demand/supply` clamped to 1 prices a *perfectly balanced* market at the buyer's worst price — one mine feeding one mill used to clear at $399.40 against a $400 ceiling. Here a matched pair splits the band. Supply is flow plus a slice of the stockpile, never the stockpile itself: pricing off inventory alone is circular — low price, withhold, bigger inventory reads as more supply, lower price — and measured that way food collapsed to the floor in every scenario including a genuine shortage.

Neither end of a band is a constant: both are read off the world's own prices every month, through the exchange rate, so a devaluation is import inflation mechanically — and an incentive to substitute. And since 16 September neither end is a single number either: each is the world's own price plus, or less, the cost of moving one unit, so the band a city faces is three quarters freight and one quarter the world's margin, and the freight is a price a railway can win back — see [transport](#18-transport--vehicles). The shops buy local food first and import the shortfall; the mills take local ore first and scrap for the rest. One clearing pass runs every month: flow goods are made, seller-priced goods sold, each traded good priced, offered, bid for and allocated **pro rata on both sides**, then imported or exported, then the stockable goods made. Every fill is a trade; nothing in these classes moves money. The households are not a sector and cannot bid in a strike: they take cars off the makers' shelf at the struck price and import the rest, through the same door the city uses for building material, and a month's purchases are demand for next month's strike. A good with a floor of zero — a van, a wagon set — strikes at exactly zero when nobody here wants one, and a saved zero is restored as zero, because for one build a guard against a missing figure dropped it and a reloaded city read a mid-band price in its place.

### What a household eats

Until September 2026 one good called *Food* did all of this: a unit was a person fed for a month, everything they ate, and every question about a city's diet had that one answer. The shelf is itemised now, and what goes into the basket is decided by income rather than by a dial.

**Engel's law** is the first half: as a household gets richer the *share* of its money spent on food falls while the *amount* rises. **Bennett's law** is the second: the calories move off starchy staples onto meat, dairy, fish and produce. That is why grains carry a *negative* income elasticity — a staple is an inferior good, and a household eats less rice as it gets richer, not more.

Neither law is told what to do at the top of the ladder. A basket is scaled by the **lesser** of what a household can afford and what it can eat, so a poor household is money-limited and goes hungry while a rich one is calorie-limited and buys dearer food instead of more. The falling food share at the top is something the model *produces* rather than something it is given — which matters, because the first draft typed that share in as a constant and produced households whose calories went *down* as they got richer.

There is a third axis that is not income at all. **Convenience food is bought for time**: a working parent buys it at any income, and an out-of-work parent with the same children and the same money does not, because what they are short of is money and what they have is afternoons.

Income is measured in **multiples of what bare subsistence costs** rather than in dollars, so a currency reform cannot move it and the number means something you can say out loud: *this household can afford four times the calories it needs to survive.* The shops stock one shelf for the whole city, averaged over its households by *headcount* rather than by spending — a shelf stocked for money would carry the rich end's fish and fruit for a city of labourers.

> **The shelf is thirteen pantries**
>
> A shop can sell a basket only if it has all of it: what it can serve is the good that runs out first, which is Liebig's barrel on a shelf. That is also how a units bug was caught — shelf room was still sized in *units of food* when the goods became *kilograms*, and one person-month is exactly 50 kg of them, so every shop in the city delivered 20% of demand for ever. A city with roads and a city without scored identically until it was found; afterwards, **87% against 31%**.

When the shelf was itemised all thirteen were imported. Eleven of them can be made at home now: the ovens bake bread and bakery goods out of crops and export what the city cannot eat; the farms make dairy and eggs, meat, vegetables and fruit; the plants make the five processed goods out of meat, vegetables, grains and crops. Grains and fish still only ever come off a ship. And since 18 September the shelf has a second buyer: the kitchens buy the same thirteen in the reference basket's proportions and sell them cooked, one ninetieth of a person-month a plate.

> **The hunger measure was reporting zero in a city that was starving**
>
> Until 17 September the figure read *sold over the shops' own demand*, and the shops' demand was already the least of coverage, want and what could be afforded — the shops' performance against a queue the shops had themselves decided they could serve. At month 3,840 of seed 0 the households planned 21,446,946 baskets, the shops could serve 177,760 people, and the line said 76%. A basket is one person-month, so the city wanted a hundred and twenty-two baskets a head and was allowed one. Honest: **58% of people short, 1.4% of the groceries asked for**. Not a reporting change: the hungry feed the sick rate, which feeds the labour supply, and it had been fed a zero. Turning it on cost the default seed 11% of its population and 14% of its GDP — revealed, not caused — and showed a cascade nobody had seen, sickness 12.9% to 34.5%, of which hunger is eight points and *the unburied fifteen*. The basket count is floored to a whole basket, because dividing money by money and keeping the fraction broke the currency-reform twin 1.5e-06 at a time.

## 8. The private sector

*Nobody tells businesses what to build. Each of the fifteen sectors measures a different signal, projects it six months out, and expands only if the new capacity would service its own debt.*

```
the brake   estimated monthly profit ≥ monthly interest × 1.25
```

A business test, not a credit limit: the lender is willing, the business should not be. Alongside it: one order at a time per sector, never more than twelve months of the *whole city's* construction output, and a 5% headroom target so nothing expands into capacity it already has.

| Sector | Watches |
| --- | --- |
| Real estate | jobs plus jobs under construction — never population, which is its own echo |
| Retail | a twelve-month population trend, capped at housing that exists or is being built |
| Industry | shop coverage against output; refuses outright if price is below cost |
| Construction | its own backlog, expanding past nine months of it |
| Heavy industry | spare ore — mines first, mills after |
| Mining | unmined deposits, so geology gates it and the player controls the gate |
| Materials | the sites' outstanding orders and the repair draw, on a three-year view |
| Business services | seats it could actually staff — the world's appetite for the work is unbounded, so the brake is people, not demand |
| Manufacturing | the price of steel, which is the whole of it — 61% of a fabricator's revenue |
| Agriculture | the mills' crop bill against the price of the ground a field has to stand on — and refuses while anybody in the city has nowhere to live |
| Food processing | what the city already eats of its five goods, less what it can already supply, valued at each good's export floor — never a forecast, and never the export market, because the band is narrower than the processing step; scores every template it owns, not the one that makes its planning good |
| Rail | the freight nobody is carrying — it will not lay a line under 60% used, Materials' lesson relearned the afternoon a spur went up in a town of four hundred houses |
| Automotive | the parts — one new plant may want at most a quarter of everything the city fabricates, because "spare" was the wrong word and cost a fixture three hundred months |
| Luxury retail | the queue at the door: the margin the counters are striking against the pieces the households want |
| Restaurants | the queue at the door: meals asked for against the tables there are, and a kitchen values itself, because nothing else can |

### The eighth, ninth and tenth, and why they are different

The first seven sectors all sold to the city. **Business services** and **manufacturing** sell to the world, which is what broke a two-hundred-year plateau: a city whose every customer lives in it can only grow as fast as it grows. **Agriculture** is the other direction — it sells to the mills, and it is the only sector whose real cost is the ground it stands on.

| Sector | In | Out | Where the money goes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Business services | almost entirely people; 250 sq ft of lot a head | support, back-office and engineering work, by the seat-month, at $5,500 / $8,600 / $14,600 | payroll 66.3% / 65.2% / 55.2% |
| Manufacturing | steel, local or imported | fabricated steel and machinery, flow not stock; export only until the assembly plants arrived | steel 61.0%, or wages 49.1% at the Machine Works |
| Agriculture | land heavily, labour and power barely | `CROPS`, to the mills | labour a seventh of a field's sale, power a five-hundredth |

**The engineering office is gated on a licence**, not on money: it will not open without spare licensed engineers for half its gated posts (`LICENCE_COVER_TO_OPEN = 0.5` — thirty-nine of them; thirty-eight is one short), and the only way to make one at home is an Institute of Technology. **Steel got its first domestic customer** and with it an import ceiling of 1.284 against the mills' export floor of .847, a 1.52× wedge that decides whether fabricating here pays at all: 1.55% of build cost a month on imported steel at the ceiling, 3.28% on steel at the mills' floor. **The mills got an input cost** — they used to make food out of nothing, on margins of 72–77% against every other plant's 28–31%.

> **The farmland dial**
>
> `TaxPolicy.FARMLAND_RELIEF` assesses farmland at use value rather than development value, on the land half only — barns are still taxed as buildings. It defaults to full relief and says in dollars what the relief costs. Six grain farms on \$112m of ground: **\$151,496 a month with no relief, \$11,295 with full relief.** Without it a field cannot outbid a warehouse for the same acre, and by month 4,002 at \$66 a square foot there are no fields left — ten greenhouses, and the two founding mixed farms.

### How an expansion is paid for

In a fixed order, every month: **sell shares** if the register says the company should be raising equity, **spend the till**, **call money home from abroad**, and only then **borrow**. A company under a year old sells half of what it plans; a company with nine good months raises toward its equity target; a company with a bad year raises nothing and borrows nothing.

### Capacity retires, and distress retires it faster

Six consecutive losing months, genuinely spare capacity by a 25% margin, and nothing on site — then the biggest holding is thinned, never past what is actually in use, never more than a quarter in one month. The streak is carried in the save, because forgetting it made scrapping save-scummable.

Separately, a firm that **cannot pay** sheds plant: twenty-four months of losses *and* a negative balance after the credit desk has already refused it. Six months killed every founding plant in testing; two years is the runway a real business gets. Occupied homes and the bank are never scrapped. A mine over a worked-out deposit now closes inside a year instead of borrowing to pay its crew for three — which makes the bust when the ore runs out sharper, and lets the bank survive it. And a distressed landlord can no longer demolish a city out from under it: the railway's bigger business cycle pushed Real Estate into distress deep enough that it **sold 5,800 of a city's 13,272 homes in seven months** and left 1,137 households with nowhere for a hundred and forty, because the retirement rule asked whether the segment had spare doors and a segment's slack is spread over four sizes. It is guarded, not fixed: nobody sells a door while the housing match says somebody has nowhere, and the proper fix — slack per size — is on the list.

> **Two banners exist because these fail silently**
>
> **Builders being laid off** — construction with no orders shrinks to fit, and everything you build runs through those crews. **Nowhere to build** — the private sector asks for land every month, is told no, and waits. Measured at 120 consecutive months in one ordinary run.

## 9. The owners & the exchange

*For most of the project's life the corporate sector had no owners: it made money, held it, and nothing ever moved it out. Sixteen companies have a share register now — the fifteen sectors and the bank — and a market to trade them on.*

### The register

Every company is founded with shares issued to the city's households at $1,000 each against its book equity. A company reads its own record before it asks for money: **new** under a year, **good** at nine profitable months and not declining, **bad** at six or fewer or a losing year, normal otherwise. Its **equity target** starts at 30% of assets and rises with how volatile its income has been, capped at 70%; a new company aims at half. Households subscribe first — a cell with no debt, no lockout and three months of disposable income banked puts 30% of the excess in — and the world takes the rest, but only if the yield clears the world rate plus three points.

**Forty percent of a positive month is paid out**, from the till, or from the company's own money abroad if the till is short. A share is priced at the higher of book equity and the dividend capitalised at the world's required return, per share.

### The exchange, and the bank as dealer

The bank's trading desk is the counterparty on every trade, and quotes nothing when the bank is dead. It quotes around fair value, its own book moves the quote, it never sells what it does not hold, and it marks what it holds at the lower of the quote and fair value. Its book is capped at a multiple of the bank's equity, which is money — and until 18 September that cap was the one figure in the exchange a currency reform did not divide. It is re-struck each month *after* the households settle, so for the first half of every month a reformed city's desk believed it had a hundred times the room it had; a household with no savings and a grocery bill it could not meet borrowed in the plain city and sold $1.03 of shares in the reformed one, and from there household debt was 4.2% apart in one month and the exchange rate with it. The bisect blamed the fourteenth sector's inventory term, and the term was right: it had moved GDP, GDP had moved what the desk's book was worth against its limit, and a cancellation that had been landing on one side of zero started landing on the other. A bisect names what perturbed a fault, not what the fault is; a latent member of that family is not a harmless one, it is one nobody has perturbed yet.

```
mid = fair × clamp(1 − 0.25 × (dealerShares − demand) / scale, 0.50, 5.00)
bid/ask = mid ∓ half of a 2% spread
```

A month on the market runs in order: **emigrants sell** on the way out; **the world trades on yield**, never in a company under a year old; **households buy** the best yield above the deposit rate plus a point, spending 5% of their excess savings; then **companies buy themselves back** — a tenth of the company a year, only after a good year, only with six months of operating cost still in the till, and if the market is more than 10% over fair value the money goes out as a **special dividend** instead. A household short of money sells its shares before it borrows. Shares split at a hundred times their founding price, and a cumulative split factor keeps the price history readable per founding share.

The player does not trade. What the player sees is the desk's disclosure on the bank's income statement, its inventory at the mark on the balance sheet, an *Its owners* block on every company — quote, yield, market value, how much the desk holds, special dividends, buybacks, splits — a price chart per company, each household cell's shares at market, and the foreign share of each register on the balance-of-payments page.

**The desk foots, since 19 September.** Its opened lines on the bank's statement had left out the term that is usually the largest — the change in the mark on what it holds — so a loss sat over sub-lines that did not add to it. *Re-marked what it holds* (`Bank.getMarkChange()`) is a line of its own now, and when it is the bulk of a loss the note says why, which is Jerus's question — *"explain to me the trading desk, cause a bunch of times it's losing billions"*: with buyers it cannot fill it quotes up to five times fair value to draw sellers, and it marks what it holds at the lower of the quote and fair value, so a wave of emigrants selling into a bubble costs it the difference the same day. `BankCheck` asserts the lines plus the re-mark equal the total, and on a played city they did in 120 of 120 months. Whether a dealer should *bid* at a quote it does not believe in is Jerus's. Since 0.7.1 the same desk also buys back the city's paper from the households, at the month's market value off the curve.

> **What it was worth**
>
> Eight seeds against the batch before it: GDP $65M → $77M a month, worst unemployment 46% → 37%, exports $104M → $124M, the currency inside 3.5% of parity, dividends to households $3–18bn → $30–56bn a run, every company home-owned in six seeds of eight — and **bank failures 10 → 0**, because the trading desk is a business and a profitable one, and a sector that has just paid its owners borrows for its next mine.

## 10. Labour & schools

*A wage used to be one of six constants, copied in once at startup. Labour is a market now, skill is an axis, and a school is the only way to make a doctor at home.*

### Four bands, one price each

```
NONE < DIPLOMA < COLLEGE < UNIVERSITY       // substitution runs downward only
tightness = posts / qualified supply        // per band; a band's surplus cascades into the one below
target    = minimumWage × ratio[job] × clamp(tightness^0.5, 0.70, 4.0)
wage     += (target − wage) × 0.12          // 90% of a shortage prices in over 18 months
```

The **minimum wage is the base** of the whole ladder, so one Policy dial moves every wage in the city, the treasury's own payroll included. Because the unskilled base *is* the floor, an unskilled glut cannot be priced away — it clears in people instead, which is exactly what a binding minimum wage does. Wages also chase the cost of living in full, both directions, over 24 months, and since 0.6.11 a harness holds them to it: `LabourCheck` runs 240 months of steady inflation and asserts every month that the wage index moves exactly `DRIFT_PER_MONTH` of the way toward the published price index, through a currency reform and a reload, and on all eight seeds every one of 144 checkpoint readings sits at the level the two-year lag implies — the one-third overshoot measured on 15 September does not reproduce. Students and prisoners are out of the supply while they are away, and the pool is what is left when filled posts are taken off the labour force — an identity, not a second count.

**Gated jobs carry a licence premium** on top of their band's: posts over licence holders, same elasticity, never below one, the pair capped at 4×. A hospital with no medical school pays its doctors over the graduate band — measured at 1.26× against a band in glut at 0.83× — and that price is what draws licensed arrivals and sends graduates back to school.

### Nine schools, and a pipeline

| Stage | Takes | Produces | Course |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| Elementary, Middle, High | children and teens | a diploma, at the *narrowest* stage's coverage | 4 + 3 + 5 yr |
| Community College | diploma-holders | college graduates | 24 mo |
| University | diploma-holders | university graduates | 48 mo |
| Medical, Law, Business, Technology | university graduates | a licence for one job type — raises nobody's band | 84 / 36 / 24 / 48 mo |
