A city that has run out of ground and not out of money builds one; a city with ground to spare never should — which is the first real answer this game has had to its own late-game wall. **Every mode is a relief on an unchanged baseline**, and that is the design rather than an implementation detail: a city with no highway and no transit computes exactly the load it computed yesterday and degrades on exactly the curve it degraded on. A highway relieves freight, not by carrying more but because a tonne of ore on a grade-separated road does not share a junction with a school run — bulk by 40%, goods by 15%, commuters not at all. Transit takes people off the road entirely, and three things stop it being the answer to everything: at most 65% of commuters ever ride, whatever is built; what transit can carry is capped at twice the road capacity under it, because buses are road vehicles and a metro station needs a street outside it — *a city that builds a metro and no streets gets a metro nobody can reach*; and it never touches freight. Measured on a load of 10,000 in the played mix: 5,590 riders with room to spare, 4,800 with fewer streets, 800 with none, and with the best of everything **the road still carries 39%** of what it would. The road can be halved and it can never be deleted. It is also why the stream split matters to a business: an office and a mill on the same jammed road read 74% and 47% against the road's own 42%, because the mill beats the road by exactly as much of its own traffic as rides the tram, and a lorry in a jam is in a jam. A sector with nothing standing reads the city's own blend rather than a clean road, because the planner costs a first plant at the sector's operating rate and a congested city was cheerfully building plants a 38% road said it could not afford.

**A fare is a price, not a charge.** Nobody chooses to be policed and a patient in a clinic is not shopping; the person on a bus chose to be, and can choose a car instead. So the ridership ceiling is what a *free* system would carry and the fare walks it down on a straight line to nobody at the maximum: free, 5,590 riders; at the default, 5,311; at the ceiling, none. And the two lines move against each other, which is the whole decision — six times the fare takes $58,695 a month instead of $13,276 and puts 1,398 more cars on the road. Jerus asked for a dial that can be made profitable *"by alot"*; it can, at a ridership the city may not want. The fare is money, so a reform moves it — the twenty-third of that family and the first caught in the same edit that created the field — and the ridership curve is written against the cap rather than against dollars, so a reform moves both and nobody changes their mind about the bus. Two things were found on the way: nothing in the infrastructure category had ever had a job, so nobody had written a line to pay one, and a Metro Line is 828 posts; and the fare was charged once a month against a constant that says *a single journey*, so a monthly pass cost $2.50 against a $3,460 wage, seven hundredths of one percent, and the buses could not have paid for themselves at any fare a player would set. That was the transit loss the list had carried as a balance problem. It is 40 journeys a month now — out and back, twenty days — a pass is $100 or 2.9% of an unskilled wage, and the dial stays per ride because that is the number a person on a platform recognises.

> **The fare was collected from nobody**
>
> From the day transit was built until 16 September the city credited itself the fare and debited no household. Nobody saw it because **nothing had ever built a bus**: the playtest's advisor answered every jam with tarmac, so four thousand months a seed, eight seeds a run, not one city ever carried a passenger, and every fixture that needed a road bought a road. The first ensemble in which the advisor bought a Bus Network failed the money audit on all eight seeds, and the residual was the fare to six decimals — 2,186 riders at $2.50 is $5.47, and the audit said 5.465207. *A harness cannot check a thing nobody does.* `MoneyCheck`'s own header says every money bug this codebase has had was a flow with one side, and the twenty-ninth harness could not see this one because its city had no buses. It builds three now. Fixing it found its sibling at once: `setTransit` was missing from the load path, the fifth sighting of that shape, invisible until the fare became real money.

### The railway

Rail is the twelfth sector, and the business that wants to be paid the freight every price in this game has always had inside it. Jerus: *"the freight cant reach zero cause freight needs profit, its its own sector… it wants and will do everything possible to stay profitable and maximize profits. freight money goes to that sector."* There were two ways to write that and only one keeps the audit honest. Paying the railway out of the band would have a payment the books record as going abroad in fact going to a company in the city. So **the band carries only what the lorries still move, and the railway bills the shipper at home**, like any other supplier of a service — the invoice goes on the shipper's input line, where freight belongs in anybody's accounts, the money never leaves the city, and the VAT falls out for free because the ledger already credits a purchase at the supplier's own rate.

```
what a shipper pays a unit  = (1 − share) × baseFreight     // still to the lorries, inside the band
                            + share × quote × baseFreight  // to the railway, on its invoice
allowed  = what a month costs to run + 1.2% of the track it has sunk
quote    = clamp(allowed / what it would bill at the lorry rate × scarcity, 0.30, 1)
```

**A shop's pricing rule cannot price a utility**, and the measurement is what said so. Written first as Retail's shelf — cost plus a quarter — it quoted 32% of the lorry rate, earned $4.5m a month on ten billion of track, and was written down six times: a railway's running cost is a fraction of its capital, so a mark-up on running costs allows a return of nothing on the track. It prices like a regulated network now, running costs plus 1.2% a month on the rate base, floored at 30% of the lorry rate because rail is cheaper than a lorry and not free, capped at one because nobody ships by rail at more than the lorry charges, lifted up to 1.6× by what it cannot carry. It settles at 38–43%. Building too much rail does not make freight cheaper; it makes a railway that cannot pay for itself, and `RailCheck` asserts that a network with four times the track it needs pins at the lorries' price and earns less on four times the capital. The link that falls out of it is real and welcome: **a railway earning 1.2% a month on money that costs it 1% is barely a business, so dear money is what keeps a city's trade band wide**. And the band alone was lying to the sectors: at a 92% quote on 92% of the traffic it said steel's wedge had fallen from 52% to 11% when the shipper had saved eight per cent, because the railway's invoice was not in it. Every place that asks *is this worth exporting* reads a net price now; every place that settles a trade reads the band; with no railway the two are the same number to the bit.

**Track is half a railway.** Capacity is the lesser of the track laid and the wagon sets to run it, at 2,500 tonnes a set and a twenty-year life, so track with no locomotives carries nothing: a Rail Spur is twenty sets, $48m of rolling stock on a $140m spur, and a mature city's million tonnes of track is 420 sets and about 1¾ sets a month of replacement for ever, which is half a Locomotive Works running. Rolling stock is a *pantry* rather than an input — that one line is what makes a bought set accumulate into a fleet instead of vanishing into a month's production — and a save from before trains has trains, because it was hauling, so it had locomotives. The railway will not lay a line under 60% used, Materials' lesson relearned the afternoon a spur went up in a town of four hundred houses and a bank failed over it. It relieves 75% of the bulk it carries off the road, never all of it, because the last mile off a siding is a lorry and a spur reads as 94% trucks; bulk goes before goods, which decides almost nothing today because bulk is 99.7% of the tonnage crossing the boundary. Every tonne it hauls burns $30 of fuel in the world's money, a real import before there is any oil good, so the day `OIL` is a good nothing else changes.

> **What a railway is worth**
>
> Eight seeds, four thousand months each: population **113,178 → 178,975 (+58%)**, GDP **$416.8M → $711.2M a month (+71%)**, per seed 32–91% and 14–113%. On the default seed steel's net wedge goes from 51.6% of the world price to 25.9%. And it is a healthy business in all eight: zero write-downs, zero loss months, the best credit rate in the game, and in seven of eight no debt at all. Three rungs — 50,000, 200,000 and 500,000 tonnes a month at $140m, $520m and $1.24bn — $2,800 of capital per tonne a month on a spur and $2,480 on a terminal, and a terminal nearly three times a Coal Power Plant on the ground, which is the land trade Jerus asked for.

### The vehicles

**Automotive is the thirteenth sector, and it is not for the cars.** Ore becomes steel, steel becomes fabricated steel and machinery, and until 16 September both left, because nothing in the city bought a beam or a machine. An assembly plant is the first thing that does — the fourth link of a chain that stopped at three — and the chain cannot be shortcut: fabricated steel is deliberately not importable, so a city with money and no fabrication shop cannot be in the car business, it can only buy cars. Machinery can come off a ship, at the ceiling its own header had predicted for the day something here bought one, because a car is three and a half tonnes of fabricated steel and four hundred kilos of machinery and the bulky input is the one a city must make. **Cars export; vans and locomotives do not**, from three measurements of one failure: allowed to sell wagon sets to the world, the playtest built **19 Locomotive Works**, 9,880 posts in a city with 25,102 jobs; allowed to sell vans, **240 Commercial Vehicle Plants** shipping 36,000 vans a month; and it was already building 179 Fabrication Works and zero Machine Works. An unbounded export market at a fixed floor means the single best export is built for ever and nothing else ever is; bounded world demand is the general fix and is still its own batch. A plant may draw at most a quarter of what the city fabricates, because the first supply gate asked the mills' question — is there spare local supply — and nothing fabricated is ever spare when the world will take all of it; a $172m Assembly Plant sank in month seventeen of a fixture that was measuring tuition, and the harness was right. Eight seeds: GDP $711.2M → $758.8M a month, up in six of eight; seed 0's mature city runs 84 Assembly Plants on 23% of its fabrication.

**The cars are the fourth mode, and the only one that costs.** Highways, transit and rail are all reliefs on an unchanged baseline; a car is the opposite, and it has to be, because the baseline this network always computed was an unmotorised city, unlabelled. It is named now rather than moved:

```
onRoad        = (commuters − riders) × (1 + ownership × (3.0 − 1))     // exactly 1 at zero ownership, to the bit
willingToRide = (1 − ownership) + ownership × 0.75 × jam             // jam is a memory of the commute, a quarter a month
```

Only the people still driving pay it, so a city that motorises *and* builds transit is not charged twice for one journey, and that is what closes Jerus's loop: *"people drive until the road is full, then take the tram."* A car owner rides nothing on a clear morning and three quarters of them ride at a standstill — motorise, nobody rides, it jams, they ride, it clears — read off a memory of the commute rather than last month's road, or it is a two-month oscillator. Transit is a **ceiling on ownership, not a brake on adoption**, and the difference is the whole of whether a player has a move: on the rate it only delays, on the level a well-served city tops out at half a car per household for ever. What motorising costs, eight seeds against the same build with adoption off: **191,194 people and \$848.3M a month at 80% road, against 176,228 and \$695.7M at 73%**, cars in 60% of households and 37% of commuters riding — and the chain is not congestion alone: a worse road costs every new plant at a lower operating rate, marginal projects stop clearing the interest test, business borrowing collapses (\$6.6bn lent against \$18.5bn, the bank at 45% of capacity instead of 77%), Manufacturing's assets fall from \$23.4bn to \$6.3bn, exports fall 26%. A six-point road ratio, compounded over three centuries. `CAR_LOAD_AT_SATURATION = 3.0` is the one constant here that is a game decision rather than a measured one. The advisor learned to buy a bus the same day, and what decides between six candidates is the catalogue: each is costed in trips taken off the road per dollar — a gravel road 900 for \$2,326k against a bus network 2,500 for \$12,000k times the car factor — so a bus loses outright in a city where nobody drives and wins once about half the households own a car. Nobody chose that crossover.

**The vans are the fifth throttle, and the first one a business buys.** Energy, water, road and health all arrive; a lorry is the sector's own capital, sized from a measurement: a city of 106,612 moves 1,169,640 tonnes a month at nameplate, both sides of the door, which at 120 tonnes a vehicle is a fleet of about ten thousand, one commercial vehicle per eleven people, and eighty a month of replacement for ever. Built once without teeth, every ratio in the measured city read 100.0%, because vans are importable and a sector asking for a fleet got one in a month; you cannot put a thousand lorries on the road in a month, so a fleet is built up at an eighth a month and a firm short of its own lorries hires haulage — slowed to 60%, not stopped. Re-measured: 132 sector-months short, worst 65%, every growing sector hitting it and none stopped. A save from before vans owns a fleet, on the railway's own flag: it was moving steel, so it had lorries. And it is what finally gives the Commercial Vehicle Plant a customer.

*What the whole vehicles arc costs a mature city — eight seeds, 4,000 months each*

| Build | Population | GDP a month | Roads |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| No cars, no vans | 191,194 | $848.3M | 80% |
| Cars | 176,228 | $695.7M | 73% |
| Cars and vans | 165,914 | $673.3M | 75% |

About 13% of population and 21% of output against a city where nobody owns anything to move with — for two industries and three decisions it did not have. The households' side of the cars, who buys one and who borrows for it and who sells it last, is in [people](#2-people).

### The instrument panel

Nine batches of transport shipped before any of it was on a screen: the road carried three streams and showed one number, the fare was a real dial with a real elasticity and nothing in the game could turn it, the railway repriced itself every month and told nobody, and a mill running at 65% because it had not taken delivery of its lorries looked exactly like a mill running at 65% for no reason. **Infrastructure** is the twelfth tab on the rail since 0.6.5, after Services because that is where the eye goes looking for it, with four pages that each answer a question somebody actually asks. *Roads*: why is my throughput 73% — the free-flow curve as a banded meter, the three streams as a table with what one trip of each kind costs the street after the highways and the railway have taken their cut, then the cars. *Transit*: the three ceilings and the lowest wins, the two things that walk it down, the books, and the dial. *The railway*: track against the sets that track needs, what it hauls and off which stream, what the rule allows against what it billed, and a box that tells an over-built railway so. *Freight*: the band good by good with what is left of the wedge after rail, the month's bill split into the half billed at home and the half that leaves inside the band, and every sector's fleet — the first time the fifth throttle has been visible anywhere. The fare is the one control, staged like every other policy dial, with a preview that shows riders, fares, net cost and the trips that go back onto the road, and that says plainly what it cannot preview: the second round, where a worse road puts some of them back on the tram. Nothing on the screen builds anything; a second place to buy a building is a second place to maintain. Cars show in both places, on Population beside the household's other assets and on Roads beside the congestion number they explain. The screen shipped without anyone looking at it — the only JavaFX natives here are the Windows build and a Java window cannot be put in the screenshot allowlist — so `InfrastructureCheck` gained a ninth section that walks every accessor the four pages call, in the four city states that break screens, and asks the two questions a renderer cannot survive the wrong answer to: is it finite, and is it inside the range the label claims.

## 19. The screen, time, saves, logs

*The main menu is gone. Twelve destinations sit on a rail down the left — Build, Land office, Population, Services, Infrastructure, Sector economy, Government economy, Finances, The bank, Trade & the world, Policies, Reports — on screen from every screen, with the gear at the foot for anything that leaves the city. A new or loaded city opens on Build, the one screen a player who does not yet know what they are doing can do something on. Pressing a rail button you are already on takes you back to that rail's own front page rather than doing nothing, so there is always a way out of a sub-page without knowing which one you came in by.*

The four red banners became an **inbox**: one live notice per condition, raised from the city's own state rather than restored from a record, carrying this month's figures and one button that goes to the screen that fixes it. A resolved notice gets no button. Services carries a Safety area beside the utilities. The Reports screen records sixty-odd series with one heading per group — including *The dead*, which plots the running totals by band since the city was founded, the orphans and the people with no home among them, and the killed — on an axis that is the window rather than forced through zero. The goods page on Reports is thirty-one rows: what a unit costs here this month, the world's band around it, and what crossed the border. There is a palette, fullscreen, keyboard shortcuts, and Resume loads the autosave on a cold start instead of drawing an empty city.

The money came onto the screen with it. The strip carries prices and the exchange rate beside the cash since 0.6.10. The Money page under Finances is the central bank's balance sheet in the player's words — issued and retired this month, printed since founding, the remittance, what the defence has spent, and M0 and M2 with a year of each. The monetary page under Policies carries the dial and its chips, what the rule would set and where the dial stops, the autopilot, the holdings dial, the advances ceiling, the real rate and what savers earn in real terms. The borrow page lists the curve one row per maturity and steps a term loan's chips by ten, the book page says who holds each bond, and the Trade tab's forces page shows the four terms that move the rate. The Government tab's bridge opens into the treasury's journal and lists the arrears by line, and the bank's desk foots. And the People tab's *EI paid this month* reads what the treasury paid since 0.7.3, after the docs pass found it reading next month's bill, while the People and Summary screens read the care coverage the month actually used rather than one worked out from the beds.

### The interface is a package

Until 18 September every screen was one class: `UserInterface.java`, 25,098 lines, 492 methods, a hundred banner sections, and a session working on the bank had to carry the policy tab's text in the same window. It is nineteen files in `ui/` now, and the model never imports it. `UserInterface` is the window — the stage and its theme, the clock and the speed ladder, the two strips, the rail and the inbox, the save and settings dialogs, the time-skip dialog, the scroller every screen draws into — at about 4,000 lines. Every tab is a class of its own, `BankScreen`, `PolicyScreen`, `PeopleScreen` and so on, its banners moved verbatim with a scripted `ui.` prefix wherever it reaches the window, the Infrastructure tab drawn by `ServicesScreen`, and the left panel's content — the summary, the dashboard, the problem list — is `SummaryScreen`. What every screen shares is four toolkit classes of stateless helpers, `Money`, `Statement`, `Pieces` and `Levers`, reached through an `import static` so that not one of their call sites changed. Twelve model members and two imports were the whole cost of the boundary. The move was mechanical — a dry run prints the couplings and the compiler catches what the script missed — and the one thing the compiler cannot check is the standing rule of this interface: **the month arrives on a clock, so every panel is rebuilt under the player and must restore its own scroll position**. Opening every tab on the split found three small things: the fare dial carried the player to the Policy tab the moment it was let go, because the staged-lever slider redrew the policy screen by name; the Build tab scrolled twice as fast as every other, because it is the one screen whose content sits straight in the page and a wheel floor meant for a notch was raised on every delta of a burst; and the Reports tab moved under the pointer when a line was ticked, because the legend grows a block per line, so that one page keeps its position as pixels from the bottom.

### The statement opens

Jerus: *"can you make it so in the UI when you click on revenue or cogs, it expands and shows the individual items."* One figure that is really ten is a figure a player can read and cannot act on. Four lines on every sector's income statement open now — **Revenue** by good, split city and abroad; the **cost of sales** by good, split city and imported; **Wages** by pay tier, with posts; and **Sales tax remitted**, charged, at the border and credited — and underneath them is a `Sector.Split` per good, booked from the trade rather than reconstructed from units times price, because a local sale and an export clear at different prices in the same month. The first thing it showed was that the city's own bakeries were shipping 62% of what they baked at the world's floor while the shops bought imported meat, fruit and fish by the half-million. A disclosure that discloses nothing is worse than none: a line with one good and nothing shipped does not open, because the caret would promise a breakdown and then repeat the figure above it — and the rule about how many rows there are has to count the rows, since Construction sells no goods at all and fell straight through a rule about goods to draw a caret onto one row that repeated its total. That *other revenue* turned out to be two businesses under one label, work recognised off the order book and this month's repairs billed to every standing building, and a city whose building work has stopped and whose repair income is still growing is a city that has finished growing. The parts are frozen into the statement when it is struck, like the per-good money, because a screen reading a working field late describes a month the statement above it is not about.

The same disclosure reached two more statements on 19 September. The Government tab's bridge from the budget to the treasury's cash opens its last row into the treasury's journal, with what the journal cannot explain printed under it as *Not accounted for* ([tax, policy and GDP](#11-tax-policy--gdp)); and the bank's trading desk, whose opened lines had never added up to its total because the re-mark was left out, foots ([the owners and the exchange](#9-the-owners--the-exchange)). A row with nothing to disclose stays a plain row, and the open or closed state is a field on the screen, because the panel is rebuilt every month under the player.

### Time runs on its own

There is no *next month* button. The city runs on a clock at five seconds a month (`SECONDS_PER_MONTH`) and a speed the player picks off a snapping ladder — 0.1× · 0.25× · 0.5× · 1× · 2× · 5× · 10× · 20× · 50× — with the space bar as play/pause and the arrow keys moving the ladder. The day inside the month is painted so the city looks alive between the ticks, even though nothing in the model moves until the month turns.

Three things that only matter once the month arrives unasked. A frame that takes a long time is **clamped at a quarter second**, so a stalled window cannot swallow thirty months while it was away — the worst a single frame can advance is 2.5 months. Redraw is capped at one in every 120ms, because at 50× a month lands every 100ms and the screen cannot usefully be redrawn faster than it can be read. And a panel is now rebuilt *while the player is still looking at it*, so every scrolling page has to hold its own position across the rebuild rather than snapping to the top — which took seven attempts and a trace file to get right, and is written up on its own.

The game can pause itself when something happens, and by default it does not: the setting exists, and it is off, because a clock that stops without being asked is worse than a notice that waits.

### The summary is a problem list

The summary panel used to be six fixed rows — economy, tax, labour, health, land, people. Of the sixteen problems a player can actually build their way out of it could show exactly one, health, and only as a sick rate. A city with no water, no cells and nowhere to bury its dead read exactly like a city with none of those problems.

It is two lists now. **NEEDS YOU** carries twenty conditions that have a lever, yellow near the line and red past it, each row a door to the screen that owns the fix, and each disappearing when it is solved; when it is empty it names the condition closest to its yellow line instead, so it is never blank. **HOW THE CITY IS** carries seven readings with no dial — out of work, off sick, hungry, people a month, doubled up, ground used, the currency — always present, coloured when bad, and its door goes to the screen that *diagnoses* rather than the one that fixes.

Writing it turned up a model bug that no harness had: `getEnergyRatio()` and `getWaterRatio()` both return min(supply / demand, 1), so a row keyed off them could not appear until the lights were already out. They read load — demand over supply — now, against the 75% the dashboard has called "tight" all along.

### The calendar

Month 1 is January 2000. Purely presentational, with deliberately no reverse function — nothing should derive a month from a date string.

### Skipping time

A skip takes a snapshot before, samples *every month* during, and diffs a snapshot after. Episodes cannot be reconstructed from endpoints: a city that starved for fifty months and recovered looks identical at both ends to one that never had a problem. The report counts months short of power, water, land and road capacity, months nothing was built, epidemics and their worst month, and the peak unburied — then writes plain sentences ordered by how much each should worry you.

### Saves

Ten numbered slots plus an autosave, under `%APPDATA%` on Windows and the platform equivalent elsewhere — chosen because Steam Cloud syncs from known roots and a bare home folder is not one. Writes go to a temp file, back up the existing save, then atomically move; the worst case is a stray temp file and a save one autosave old. History graphs are per slot. Autosave fires every twelve months, before any skip, and on quit.

The save format is at **27**, and its changelog is the best history the project has. Older saves always load; only the future direction is refused. Nineteen carried the household balance sheet, twenty the repriced unit of material — an old yard read at its old value — and twenty-one the sector template, which was a clean break. Twenty-two was business services, twenty-three manufacturing, twenty-four the farms, twenty-five the bank's own cost of funds, twenty-six the price index's water-marks and **twenty-seven the sixth age band** — which also made every band-indexed array save its band *names* beside its values, so the day a seventh band arrives no existing file is read at the wrong offsets. The thirteen foods went in *without* a bump, because goods have been saved by name since the sector template: a good this build does not know is dropped and says so in the log, which is what happens to an old city's warehouse of `FOOD`. And so did everything the batches of the edition before this one added — five sectors, the freight band, the three streams, the modes and the fare, the railway's quote and its locomotives, every sector's fleet, the households' cars, their investment income, the luxury baseline and the dinners they ate — because a sector is keyed by name, a market is keyed by name, and every new figure in a household cell is appended to the end of an array whose reader checks its length. A city saved before them opened with no cars, no fleets, no kitchens, and the rolling stock its track implies, which is exactly what that city was; an eleven-sector build was proved to load a ten-sector save to the cent before the first of the five shipped. **The central bank went in without a bump too**, and so did everything around it: the treasury's journal for both months and its raised counter; the two health dials, the coverage each month used and a cell slot for the share of a cell's people who could pay for care; the grant's basis and amount, the loan's rate and the tuition scale on the policy array's tail; the vault in dollars and its revaluation (slots 22 and 23 of the foreign accounts), the debt's revaluation (24), the defence (25–27) and the real rate differential with its two inflations (28–30); what the bank still owes for paper sold between the presses, under two keys; the central bank's books, the arrears, the autopilot, the policy rate boxed so that a 0% dial reloads at 0%, the holdings dial and the advances ceiling, each under its own key; who holds every bond, saved with the bond; the households' paper as the thirty-first slot of a cell, with its book ratio; and a buyback's holders outside the pools. The fold and the spend factor added nothing: the first is a rule about counts, and the second is struck again on load. A city saved by the build the last edition described opens in 0.7.3 with an empty central bank, the vault it had bought if it bought one, the bank holding all of its paper and nothing in arrears — exactly what that city was — and a city saved by 0.7.2 pays one month's EI twice on its first month, once. Between them the long sick, the people outside the families, the household record and the whole crime system went in *without* a bump, deliberately: Gson leaves a missing key alone, and a format-21 city loads with each of them empty, which is correct for that city. A big saved city comes back with only its founding constabulary and shows the crime notice until it builds a station.

### Logs

Every `println` in the game already goes to a rotating log file, because a logging system that needs a thousand edits does not get adopted. In a packaged build there is no console, so all of it previously went nowhere. Reports and graphs to the log default off, so the 2 MB log holds the crash rather than three centuries of ASCII graphs.

## 20. How it's checked

*Sixty self-hosted harnesses plus a 4,005-month playtest that audits every month, asserts money is conserved to the cent, and reloads the city repeatedly to prove a saved game and a played one agree. `AllChecks` runs all sixty-one, one JVM each, in about three minutes — 168 seconds on 22 September, in a cloud session where the one that needs JavaFX is skipped: fifty-nine green and one red line that is known and deferred, `InfrastructureCheck`'s* "and its shops can actually be supplied"*, which Jerus put down to roads:* "its fine, we will balance later." *It went green by accident on one build of 0.7.2 and red again on the next, because the fixture is sensitive to the currency. Every count and constant on this page is struck from the tree at 0.7.3; every measurement carries its date or its batch. `RealismCheck`, a probe outside the build, is the rebalance's instrument and the thing to run first if any real-world figure is questioned. And since 18 September the playtest is the gate for a refactor as well as for a mechanic: it is deterministic, two baseline runs are byte-identical, and every move out of `Game` and every comment-only pass was proved by a run that compared equal to the morning's, bar its wall-clock line.*

| Harness | Asserts |
| --- | --- |
| MoneyCheck | a prospering city and a broke, banned, taxed, importing one both conserve money to $0.00 — every dollar that leaves a pool arrives in another or crosses the border in a way the audit can name. Closing this identity found four leaks nothing else had seen, and it is what caught theft leaving the tills |
| ConservationCheck | nothing was created or destroyed — food in equals food out plus the change in stock, exactly, with no slack; electricity revenue equals what was charged; three consecutive loads into the *same* object |
| SectorBooksCheck · BooksCheck · TreasuryCheck | every sector's statement foots under one template, and every opened line adds up to the line above it, the home and abroad halves reached by a different route from the totals the VAT is struck off; every sector's operations page — 17,219 screen lines a run — reads as a figure and never as a sentinel, an infinity or a NaN, because the Agriculture screen once printed $9,223,372,036,854,775,807 in red; the government's books date to the month they happened; maintenance is an operating cost and reaches the builders as an order; the treasury's bridge foots through its journal, land and a building stay on the budget's own line and are not named twice, and what nothing explains is the first coupon's timing to the cent — net, since 0.7.3, of the coupons the households and the central bank were paid the same month, which a founding bank quoting its savers 7,567% had hidden |
| EquityCheck · ExchangeCheck | shares issued equal shares held; a dividend leaves a till and arrives in a household; the dealer never sells what it does not hold; a split does not move anybody's wealth; the register and the market survive a reload |
| LabourCheck · EducationCheck | every wage equals its PayTier at the default floor, so the old balance is provably intact; no band staffs more posts than it has people; a doctor shortage is priced on doctors; the wage index walks to the published price index a twenty-fourth a month through 240 months of inflation, a reform and a reload; nobody graduates before the course is over and somebody does once it is; each of the grant's four bases pays what it says, a loan at 5% costs a graduate exactly its interest and a prisoner nothing, and a tripled fee brings the trap back |
| BankCheck · ForeignCheck · ForeignDebtCheck · CapitalFlowCheck · MonetaryCheck · DenominationCheck | the quote is the booking; the bank pays for the city's paper at the settle, and the section fails four ways on the old order; its quoted deposit rate is never over its lending rate while the payout stands; the books balance over ten years of foreign servicing to 5e-14 and the bank bought none of it; the vault is the founders' dollars less what the defence sold, held in dollars through a fall; original sin feeds its own premium; the world's curve values a dollar bond by its months left; a run needs fragility and a shock; the Taylor principle holds; inflation falls with the rate, 1.032 points from a 3% dial to a 40% one; a reform is bit-exact and a reformed city reloads as itself, with every opened statement line divided along with its total and the desk's room in every company — which is shares — left exactly alone |
| CentralBankCheck | money made less money destroyed is the change in M0, in a month with every kind of flow in it and in every month of a played city; the bank earns exactly the dial on its reserves and pays the window a point over it; a debt-free note prices at the dial; a broke treasury draws advances and repays them first; past the ceiling the promises are paid and the rest owed, and paid down first when cash returns; the rule moves the dial and the player's hand stops it; the holdings dial buys the bank's term paper with money it makes, bends the long end by exactly the compression and never the note, sells back within the speed's months and keeps its pace across a save; the ceiling is the player's dial; a reform scales the money and not the ratios |
| HoldersCheck | at the settle the households take their share and the bank the rest; each coupon reaches each holder in its share; a household short of money sells its paper before its shares, and below face after a hike; a buyback pays every holder, and a dollar bond bought back is money leaving the country — the section fails with a residual when its audit line is deleted; a save from before the holders loads with the bank holding everything |
| CurrencyCheck | the real rate moves the currency and the inflation differential does not — ten months of 40% inflation with no outflow move it by the parity pull alone; the defence sells the vault's capacity times the month's deficit to the cent and damps by what it sold, and an empty vault damps nothing; what the dollars fetch is the central bank's equity, not money destroyed, and M0 does not move; the dial, the rule and the appetite are uncapped; past 100 the rate goes where the push takes it, and a reform scales the guards |
| PopulationCheck · HouseholdCheck · HouseholdMemoryCheck | the city fills toward its jobs, keeps taking arrivals while crowded, and sheds people only after a tier has been dying a year; every band-indexed array is saved with its band names and the legacy list of five is pinned as five, so that nobody ever "tidies" it into tracking the enum; all seventy-eight ledgers balance and survive a save by name, and a pensioner in one band draws what a pensioner in the other does; an emptied cell folds all seven of its stocks to the cent; the spending factor is exactly one less the saving response times the real deposit rate on everything above subsistence, and subsistence does not move; the rebuild keeps what it can and re-forms the rest |
| HealthCheck · SicknessCheck · DeathRecordCheck | the workforce, wage bill and payroll do not move while output falls; outbreaks fire, decay and end; graves and backlogs survive a reload; the ring of the long sick kills at the right rate and clinics stop it; the fee scale reaches the three care fees and not the funerals, a household that cannot pay goes without care and not without food, a rich city is served exactly as before, and the premium lands to the penny; every death is attributed to a band and the running totals carry across a gap |
| OutsideCheck | the labour-pool identity holds to a person; a claim runs exactly twelve months, and is paid in the month it is credited; a student is out of the supply and repays after; closing the biggest employer puts its people on EI, paid the month it is credited; a row past EI that cannot pay its rent is evicted by the share unpaid, and a quarter of the evicted leave |
| CrimeCheck | K reproduces Canada's rate at Canada's coverage; every cell of the pressure table; more police is always less crime and never none; the six-month ring, a full prison and an early release; the crime pull on migration; and a bare city at 2.4× Canada's rate against a policed twin at 0.16× |
| ConsumptionCheck | the two laws across the whole income range rather than at a point; that a household off the end of the curve still eats; that a famine diet scores worse than a mixed one; that the same file at a hundred times the prices buys the same food to the gram; that the enum's thirteen prices and the data file's agree to the cent; and that the city's money and the world's are never divided into one another by accident |
| BusinessServicesCheck · ManufacturingCheck · AgricultureCheck | one per sector since the template, and each asserts the thing that sector alone can get wrong: an office refuses to open without licensed engineers and opens with them; steel clears between the mills' floor and the import ceiling once something here buys it, and the mills book a local sale for the first time; the relief reaches the land half of a field's assessment and not its barns, and a farm's worth is stated in money at the world's floor, because four farms in two units cannot share a tonnage column |
| FoodProcessingCheck | all three plants are reachable by the sector's own planner where the generic one would have seen one; a first plant is valued with its own nameplate in the supply rather than at the ceiling it will destroy; twenty points on the sales tax moves what a plant is thought to earn; meat at a farm's floor is worth more to a Meat Works than meat off a ship and the difference is most of what the works is worth; and the fixture runs until the sector is about to build rather than for a number of months, holding the sector so the state under test is reached by construction |
| TradeCostCheck · RailCheck | not one delivered price moved and freight is three quarters of the half-wedge, against a table of what the prices were that morning; every building's three loads add to its road load to the bit and the network's total is the sweep it always was; the road can be halved and never deleted; a jammed city with good transit keeps its offices working and its lorries in the jam; free transit carries the ceiling, the default fare nearly all of it, the ceiling fare nobody, and a month of riding is a share of a wage somebody would recognise; a city with no railway is the city it was to the bit on all four prices, what leaves the band plus what the railway bills is the blended rate over twenty-five pairs, every dollar of haulage is on a shipper's cost line, track with no trains carries nothing, and four times the track it needs cannot be charged for |
| CarCheck · VanCheck | a city with nobody driving is the city it was, and the factor is one exactly; a fully motorised city asks three of the road; at a standstill three quarters of the owners are on the tram and one good month does not empty it; a month of car sales is real money and the savings really left; no household owns less than none of a car or more than one; a household short of the cash still buys, on credit, the seller is paid in full and a lender found the difference; a family that cannot feed itself puts the car up and somebody buys it, and a city where everybody is selling gets the floor and nothing else; a metro built after the cars unmotorises the city to its ceiling; a sector's fleet is sized by what its plant moves, both ways through the door, one with none is slowed to the floor and not stopped, a fleet is built up at an eighth a month and wears out in ten years, and a save from before vans reads as a sector that has never been asked |
| RestaurantsCheck | a meal is a ninetieth of a person-month in both directions; empty tables charge the floor, a full kitchen the middle, a queue near the ceiling, monotone between them, and a Diner clears its wages at half its tables after the sales tax; ninety dinners feed one of a couple and a hundred and eighty feed the household, at a hundred times the price exactly the same, and a dinner is eaten once; a city that could buy anything still eats a third of its meals out; the kitchens restock off every one of the thirteen in the basket's proportions; and a queue at a door that is not there is a reason to build one |
| YearBookCheck | the year book folds each series the way that series has to be folded — a flow sums, a level takes December, a rate averages and keeps its worst month — and the file says so; a decimal point survives a French locale; and the unemployment column is the model's own rate on a played city that has somebody studying, because a harness that only checks the arithmetic will certify the wrong number |
| StaleCheck | the prose still describes the code: `tools.Stale` reads the tree and `docs/` and finds a javadoc with no member under it, prose naming a source file or a page that is not there, and a stated count of banners, harnesses or interface files that is out; a fixture with three planted lies has each one come back, a sound file has none, and the tree itself is at zero on all three — it shipped red on purpose, with 84 orphaned javadocs across 40 files, all real and all older than the tool |
| SaveFileCheck · BuildingDataCheck | a played city and a reloaded one agree figure for figure; `buildings.json` produces exactly the built-in definitions, field by field |
| …and twenty more | build menu, calendar, the carry trade, credit, GDP, history, housing, the inbox, infrastructure, investment, land, mining, new game, policy, read paths, restructuring, robustness, save slots, skip reports, water |

> **Rules the harnesses are written to**
>
> **A fixture must cause the condition, not wait for it. Assert against the model's own constants, never a literal** — a check pinned to 0.06 or 2.25 tests that nobody edited the harness. **Assert the shape of a distribution, not only its total** — an aggregate cannot see a missing category. **Count how often a new mechanic actually fires in a real run** — out-migration once shipped fully tested and fired zero times in 4,002 months, and foreign borrowing had to be told to happen. **A quantity in one unit tested against a rule that assumed another** is the shape that keeps recurring. **A fixture has to cause the condition under test, not stand next to it** — fifty-odd sightings now, the latest a fixture that measured an oven's revenue on one of its two products and reported it losing money. **When a fix is safe because some case is exactly unchanged, assert that case at zero tolerance** — a sector making one good must carry exactly 1.0 of its own cost, and that is a check rather than a comment. **A harness cannot check a thing nobody does** — the fare was collected from nobody for as long as no fixture had built a bus. **When a harness goes red on your change, ask the same question of ten fixtures before believing it is your change** — one fixture said the farms broke the currency reform; ten said the model had been carrying a coin-toss for months. **A sentinel is a value for the code to compare, never a value to print**, and the place it leaks is the screen, which was the one layer with no harness behind it — and the plainer rule beside it: play the game, because fifty-one green harnesses and a ten-fixture sweep did not find a nine-quintillion-dollar unit cost that clicking on Agriculture found in ninety seconds. **Assert the premise the whole suite stands on** — a `month++` left twice at the top of the month passed every harness in the suite, and only the playtest's month numbers gave it away; `CalendarCheck` asserts one press is one month now. **Is the field money? Then it belongs in the reform the day it is written** — a rule cheaper than the twenty-five constants of the family before it. **A held sector is held in both directions** — a planner that could demolish a harness's fixture scrapped six spurs of an over-built railway, and an assertion whose subject is decided by a planner is an assertion about the planner.

> **Decided by dust**
>
> The money-constant family — a bound written in absolute money that a currency reform walks past — is past twenty-five sightings, and since 16 September it has two relatives that are not constants at all. **The sign of a residue.** Four retired households owed minus 2.7e-29 dollars, out of the monthly rebuild handing a cell `weight × g / g`, which can come back an ulp above `weight`. The magnitude is not money and nothing reads it as money; one thing reads its *sign* — `investAbroad()` asks `debt <= 0` to decide who may keep money abroad — so four cells flipped, their paper came home at a tenth a month, the financial account moved by thousands, and the exchange rate, which is every import and export price in the city, moved with it: a city and its reformed twin ran together at 1e-13 for 158 months and were 2–4% apart a decade later. The fix is four clamps and no numbers, because a ratio cannot go stale in a new unit. *A zero-crossing test is a threshold, and a threshold on a residue is decided by luck.* **A money ratio that comes out as a physical quantity.** The car affordability test is money over money and the answer is cars, which the road, the market and the trade balance all read; `(a/100)/(b/100)` is not `a/b`, so a reformed city wanted an ulp more of a car, bought it somewhere else, and `DenominationCheck` went red on sixteen assertions. Scale-invariant in arithmetic and not in floating point, and the cure is a grain: a cell buys whole cars, and the shops sell whole baskets. The playtest flags any household position below zero at zero tolerance, every month of every seed, and was seen to fail 216 times before it was trusted.
>
> Two more sightings since. **A hair of borrowing is a discrete state** (0.6.8): the waterfall clamps a negative remainder, but a positive 1e-21 becomes a debt, and `investAbroad()` gates on `debt <= 0`; the first draft of the price at the door re-split a row's bill by its paying heads, and the reform twins parted a decade later over *interest 2.36e-21 against 0.0* in one cell. The re-split was dropped rather than touch the waterfall. **A ghost household** (0.7.2): a cell whose census count had fallen to a residue — 1e-15 households, or a real 0.3 — still held savings and was still being paid, a household to some lines and not to others, and one line divided a credit by it; `DenominationCheck` went red at a floating-point knife-edge and the trace found it. The cure is a grain again: under half a household a cell is empty, and `DenominationCheck` looks 202 times over both cities and finds no cell under half a household holding anything.

### The tree, and the prose that describes it

The tree is 211 files and 138,090 lines: one flat package plus `sectors/`, `ui/` and `tools/`. `Game.java` is the seam every system meets at, 9,277 lines and twenty-eight banner sections, and on 18 September four mechanics that already had the shape of a class left it with their text intact and their behaviour byte-for-byte unchanged — the households' car market as `Motoring`, the boutiques and the kitchens as `LuxuryCounter`, who is at risk of offending as `Offending`, what the city eats as `CityBasket` — each called from the same line of the month it always was, with every moved getter kept on `Game` as a delegation so that no caller changed. The currency reform stayed, because it redenominates twenty-two subsystems through `Game`'s own fields and that is the seam doing the seam's job. The investor, the foreign borrowing and demographics are bigger and entangled, and each would be a plan of its own.

Nobody reads those files whole. `tools/` reads the sources as text and writes `docs/`: a code map with one row per file and one page per file listing its banners and every method with its line; `dials.md`, every `static final` with its value and the sentence above it, 780 of them; `month-order.md`, the month as a numbered list of statements with where each call goes, which is what section 01 of this page is struck against; and `harnesses.md`, the 3,870 labelled assertions under their sections and which harnesses name which class — which is how it is known that nothing yet names `Automotive` or `LuxuryRetail`. `Where` finds a member or a banner by name and prints it; `SaveDump` looks inside a save without loading it. And every batch has a sixth step since 18 September, done by a context that did not make the change: a docs pass that makes every comment, header, index and count agree with the code again, because the agent that changed the code has stopped seeing the prose. Its first run found four stranded javadocs and two false headers; its mechanical half is `tools.Stale`, which found 84 orphaned javadocs on its first run and is at zero now; the half that needs judgement stays with a reader, and four comments whose numbers disagreed with their constants were decided by Jerus — *"the code is correct, the comments are the outliers."*

## 21. Open questions

*Known, measured, and written down rather than discovered later. These are decisions, not defects. Twenty-seven stood here in the last edition; three have been answered since, and the five batches of the central bank opened ten more, reconciled against the project's own list on 22 September.*

| Question | What is measured |
| --- | --- |
| The city's size is hypersensitive to a small steady drag | Seven *hundredths* of a point added to the sick rate, with no crime at all, ends two seeds **9% smaller**; at a thousandth of crime's strength another ends 16% smaller. It predates every recent batch, and it means an eight-seed median can hide or invent a 10% effect. **The first thing to look at next.** |
| A bank with no lending business | **Half answered, and the other half closed by measurement.** On the default seed on 22 September the bank lends $13.2bn of $77.9bn deposited and runs at 69% of its capacity. Since 0.7.0 its spare cash earns the policy rate at the central bank rather than the world's 2% abroad, which changes what idle money pays and not how much of it there is. Nothing borrows below what the money costs the lender now, and over sixteen seeds failures went 5.0 → 0.0 median, recapitalisation $3.8bn → $0, months run at a loss 44–58% → 3–14%. The intended next step — a real intermediary funding domestic investment out of domestic savings — was measured and dropped: the bank lends **1.87% of its deposits** at home and runs at 31–49% of the capacity it already has. The city's savings are on the order of two hundred thousand times what its productive sector wants to borrow. It is demand-limited, not funding-limited, and deposit-gathering cannot change that. The open question is what a city this rich should be able to *do* with the money. |
| Cities that empty out, and nothing notices | Over sixteen seeds, nine had a population drawdown of more than half — median worst 57%, deepest 77% — and it is present in the control build too, so it is not new. Every one of those runs reports "Nothing. Every month passed the audit." The money conserves, the books foot, and a city loses three people in four with no finding raised. **The audit has no measure of a city shrinking.** |
| Savings that cannot be spent | Read off a real screen, slot 3, month 2305, a city of 1,003,081. The 1,361 households in *out of work, EI run out* are each \$390 a month short, have **\$201,363 put by** — 516 months of cover — and have defaulted. **The reading is settled and the fix is not made**: the draw-down path is wired, and the discharge fires anyway because `discharge()` tests the *wage* against subsistence and never looks at savings — a bug in the opposite direction, and why a city with no poor people in it manufactures bankruptcies. It belongs with the supply work. Alongside it: orphan bands three orders of magnitude apart on a 2,300-month steady state. The prisoners' \$70 student loan that stood here was the balance they carried in — nothing collects a student loan except from a working family — and since 0.6.9 the freeze is the prisoner's own, no instalment and no interest. |
| The index's base period | The basket is weighted from a month two years in, and the shelf-price row below says the shelf floor holds the level at about 0.78 and it cannot fall further — so a run reading near that has been measured partly against a floor rather than against its own start. A rebased version is built and not shipped: `DeathRecordCheck` goes red on it with the orphan count moving the other way (60→73 as shipped against 59→46 rebased), which is a directional flip and wants explaining before either number is trusted. |
| The landlock predicate does not clear | `Game.isPrivateInvestmentLandLocked()` reads true at month 12 with 1,974,000 sq ft still free, and is still true at month 300. `landBlockedSectors` does not appear to be emptied, so the inbox notice "your businesses have nowhere to build" is very likely firing on cities with plenty of ground. The summary deliberately does not use it. |
| The households' trillion | **Half answered, and the half that is left is a supply question.** The hoard was diagnosed on 17 September — foreign coupons compounding abroad at 1.58% a year, \$2,649bn of them against \$584bn of every wage ever paid — and it was given somewhere to go: the coupon paid home, a wealth term in the plan, cars, boutiques and kitchens. Net worth oscillates now instead of climbing (432 → 137 → 128 → 214 months of GDP), and the default seed ends on 22 September with the households holding US\$197bn abroad against \$73.8bn at home, where one seed used to hold US\$1.1tn against \$105bn. What is left: a quarter of every plan is never delivered and the undelivered quarter is the hoard, because the city cannot sell its households what they already want to buy; and `MARGINAL_PROPENSITY` has no life-cycle behind it — a fifth of discretionary income saved for ever, by everybody, at every age, is the third leak and the only one entirely untouched. |
| The bubble | Tens of billions of household savings chasing companies worth a fraction of that, at what was then a 0% deposit rate, puts quotes at two to four times fair value until the yield falls to the deposit rate plus a point. It is the price ceiling working, and it is what a city with no lending does with its savings. A bank that lent would end it — the bank item from the other side. |
| A lockup | The smallest prison is 300 cells for $360M; a city of 15,000 needs about twenty cells. No seed has ever built one, so 2,100–2,900 people were caught over 333 years and every one of them walked — and the cities are ten times the size now: 59,189 caught on the default seed on 22 September, all of them walking, with three stations covering 46% at the end. A 40-cell lockup, or cells in the headquarters; and an advisor that ever builds a prison. |
| Rent per cell should follow the door | The housing match bills landlords by unit size and puts a pensioner in the smallest flat that fits; the household books still charge families and the retired the city's *average* door. So **Senior living alone** is the one cell in trouble in every seed — −\$46 to −\$294 a month for the first decade, \$8,970 owed at the ceiling, locked out — and since the sixth band, **Elder living alone** beside it is the one to watch first when senior care is short. The people outside the families already pay their own door share; families and pensioners do not. |
| The shelf price still has a floor doing a price's job | Retail's cost-plus shelf price cannot fall below a founding constant. The shelf is thirteen invoices now rather than one, so the cost side is real in a way it was not — but the floor is unchanged, and it is still a constant doing a price's job and still part of why the price index cannot fall past about 0.78. It is also half of why the policy rate cannot reach the index; the other half is the row on the shelf and money below. |
| Full general care is worth less than it was | A fully served adult used to die at 0.15% a year. They now die at 0.232% — the halved base rate plus a sliver of illness — because the ×3 swing is gone. The halving does not make up for the good end. The lever is the halving, not the ring. |
| The investment planner ignores every ratio | In most sectors it costs a new building at nameplate capacity — real estate is the exception and the pattern to copy. It also under-builds shops, and it has never built a college, so the student machinery is only exercised in a harness — and, since 0.6.9, in a playtest that is told to build schools (`-Dplaytest.schools=true`). |
| The supply wall | Why can the shops fill only three quarters of a plan in a city with a hundred billion of unspent demand standing in front of them? Retail's binding constraint is coverage times the operating rate, and the operating rate in the default playtest is about half. On the default seed on 22 September the shops fill **77% of the queue they could serve at all**, running at 77%, and the city gets 4.2% of the groceries it asks for; whatever is not delivered is banked, by construction, because the settle has nowhere else to put it. The kitchens are a second door and took median hunger from 36% to 22%. The dearer basket — a rich household buying a dearer basket rather than more of them, since nobody eats twice — is the only consumption item left, and Jerus's call was to take it through the new sectors first. |
| Who is playing | The playtest's advisor built five wind farms and two cemeteries for 176,000 people over three centuries, not because it ranks constraints badly but because the loop skips six to a hundred and twenty months between looks, averaging fifty-four — deliberately, the length a person actually clicks. So **every number the harness has ever reported was measured in a city in crisis from neglect**. A second player, `-Dplaytest.player=attentive`, checks in yearly with the same advice: over eight seeds **418,948 people against 148,479, $2,125M a month against $544M**, hunger 18% against 43%, sickness 7.8% against 23.1% — and a labour ceiling the neglected city never reached, at 89% fill. The default is bit-identical to before the flag, so every ensemble in the record stays comparable. And one that cannot be explained: over 600 months the *neglected* city ends bigger and richer than the attentive one while being sicker and hungrier, and over 4,000 the ordering reverses decisively. Something about the early game. |
| Bounded world demand | An unbounded export market at a fixed floor means the single best export is built for ever and nothing else ever is: 179 Fabrication Works and zero Machine Works over a run, then nineteen Locomotive Works and two hundred and forty Commercial Vehicle Plants the day those could be sold abroad. The narrow fix was to say the world does not buy vans or wagon sets; the general fix touches four sectors and would change every existing city, and it is still its own batch. |
| A concentration limit on the bank | Materials borrowed 38% of the whole book in one name to buy a plant and a fleet, and defaulted in month 70 with the bank's equity at minus $2,628. The mechanic is right; a lender with no concentration limit is one default from failing, and the households' car loans now sit in the same book. |
| A plant that loses money before interest is still lent for | On 0.7.2's path land comes free at months 127–128, Manufacturing borrows $74M against a bank whose equity is $30M for a Fabrication Works that loses money before interest, and it is written off at month 166 and its restructured remainder at 178 in seeds 0 to 3; in some seeds it rebuilds and fails again. Bank failures on the default eight went from 8 to 19, all of the rise Manufacturing's, none of it the currency's. The fix belongs in the investment rule — lending past the bank's equity for a plant that loses money before interest, and an insolvent sector rebuilding — and it is the concentration limit above, found from the other side. |
| Size-level slack in the housing retirement rule | A distressed landlord sold 5,800 of 13,272 homes in seven months because the rule asked whether the segment had spare doors and the slack was spread over four sizes. Guarded — nobody sells a door while somebody has nowhere — not fixed. Whether a given set of households fits a given set of doors is a packing question and no comparison of totals answers it. |
| Every planner assumes the ground is free | The fields plan off the crop market, the houses off the jobs, the fabricators off the steel price, the railway off the freight nobody is carrying, and none of them can see that they are bidding for the same land. The rule that stopped the farms crowding out housing is a patch on one sector, not a mechanism, and the railway and the assembly plants are the hungriest for ground the game has had. A land market the planners bid into. |
| A third of meals out, and two businesses that cannot fail | `MOST_MEALS_EATEN_OUT` is a third and nothing measures whether that is the right number; on the best seeds a quarter of the city eats out and the kitchens build to the cap. Restaurants finish seven seeds of eight with zero write-downs at 2.00% credit, the profile of Retail and Agriculture, the sectors that have never gone under — a business that cannot fail is not much of a decision. Luxury Retail is the opposite, going under more often than anything but Mining and Materials, its two buildings never sized against a city's luxury budget, and **it still has no harness of its own**: every bootstrap fault the kitchens hit had already been paid for there, and nothing names `Automotive` either. |
| A car costs nothing to keep, and its loan is a bridge | Jerus wants a car to cost something to keep, which gives *cut back expenses* something to cut and makes a financed car a real commitment; the open question is where the money lands — rent reaches Real Estate through a good and a sale, so a motoring bill needs a new good sold by Automotive, or fuel imported from the world. And a car loan with a term, if the credit cycle is meant to be felt rather than merely recorded: today's loan is repaid out of spare cash within a month or two. |
| The railway's allowed return is a constant | A regulated network's allowed return follows the cost of its money; here `TARGET_RETURN` is 1.2% a month whatever the credit desk charges, and the link runs the other way — dear money keeps the band wide. Alongside it: the railway settles at 38–43% of the lorry rate in the ensemble and has been seen quoting 99% of a lorry, which leaves shippers barely better off; and rail haulage does not reduce a sector's van need, while Construction draws its materials on demand and so reads as moving nothing. |
| What no harness looks at | The sector pages are the only screen whose text a harness reads. The city panel, the People screen, the Policy pages and the Reports page are as right as somebody's last look at them; the Infrastructure tab shipped without anyone looking at it and its layout pass is owed — a twelfth tab crowding the rail on a short window, five-column tables wider than the statement column; and the four opening statement lines build nodes directly rather than lines a check can read. The strip's two panels, the Money page and the monetary page joined them: the screens cannot run in the cloud, so they are checked by eye on the PC, and those of 0.7.2 and 0.7.3 have not been yet. Education's cost and the transit payroll are outside G, which healthcare's and the police's are not. |
| The term premium is Jerus's to settle | `DebtManager.TERM_PREMIUM_10Y` … `50Y` at 0.50, 0.90, 1.15, 1.35 and 1.50 points were set to have a curve at all, and the shape — linear from a year to ten, linear between the entries, flat past fifty — is the implementer's reading of the brief. The world's curve reads the same table, so the numbers price dollar paper too. |
| The "spread is gone" sale can hardly ever fire | The households' yield is read off today's curve, which sits on the dial, and the deposit rate is a share of what the bank's book earned, so the paper nearly always out-yields deposits and the sale does not happen in a real run; `HoldersCheck` exercises it by handing it a zero yield, a fixture standing next to its condition. And 0.7.2 saw it fire anyway: in `BankCheck`'s settle month the deposit rate rose past the paper's yield, 6.825% against 6.726%, and the desk bought $1,080k back. Whether the rule should read the coupon locked in at issue is Jerus's. |
| A failed bank's hole still goes abroad | `Bank.resolveIfFailed()` and the audit's resolution line declare the shortfall as absorbed from outside the city, though the bank's wholesale lender is the central bank's window now and the window is repaid out of that inflow at the next settle. Who absorbs a failed bank — the central bank as lender of last resort, the depositors, the treasury — is Jerus's, and the Bank tab's resolution note waits on the answer. |
| The currency's new numbers are untuned | `ForeignAccounts.RATE_PULL` 4 and `CapitalFlows.MAX_SPREAD` .25 are both marked in the source as Jerus's numbers to settle. Four was chosen because six gave the loop a gain of 1.44 and sent one seed to its guard; it buys two thirds of the support a credible real rate used to buy. And the rate term acts from month one, before the trade pressure is allowed to, which predates the batch. |
| The exchange rate goes NaN in a city with no trade | A founding left without the advisor goes NaN at month 26, on 0.7.2 and 0.7.3 alike: `pressure()`, `absorption()` and `realRateDifferential()` read NaN first, and the currency's guards pass it through, because a clamp hands a NaN straight on. Found by the 0.7.3 batch and not traced to the root. |
| Should the defence answer only a crisis? | The founders' billion goes on structural deficits, not crises: every default seed sells more than half of it and six all but 1%, while the playtest's advisor buys it back with the treasury's cash — one seed sold US\$1.29B of a US\$1B vault, and held at a 50% dial US\$625B. On the default seed on 22 September half of it was gone by month 726. A defence that waited for a run would need a rule for what a run is; the hot money's panic, a fragile position and a shock, is the nearest the model has. |
| Interest on reserves compounds without limit at a held extreme rate | Held at 30% or 50%, M0 reaches 10^8 to 3×10^14 $B while prices stay near one: spare cash earning the rate in new money that becomes spare cash, and the households' savings, earning it too, reach 10^7 to 10^14 years of income. And the central bank ends every default seed with its equity below zero, mostly the loss carried from paying interest on reserves: minus $1.1B to minus $3.3B on 0.7.2's eight, minus $2.39B on the default seed on 22 September. |
| Who gets 45% | `Bank.DEPOSIT_PASS_THROUGH` is .45 and the code pays it to savers; the comment above it quotes Jerus asking for "55% of interest income" and calls "the 45% it keeps" the margin. It is why the deposit rate carries about a quarter of the dial, and it is the cheapest lever the demand channel has. Beside it: the deposit quote's cap binds beyond the founding, 17 to 236 months of each default run, and every reader of the deposit rate sees the capped figure while the payout stands. |
| The shelf is priced by coverage, not by money | The structural reason the rate cannot reach the index. Retail's shelf sits at its floor or marks up against the shops' coverage — what it can serve, not what is wanted — so a tenth less want moves no price, and food is four fifths of the index; the counter and the table, where discretionary money goes, are not in it at all. A shelf priced by scarcity against money is the next design, and `MonetaryCheck`'s point of transmission is still mostly the currency's until it exists. |
| Onboarding | The game never states the goal or teaches its causal order — land, housing, people, jobs, industry. Every confusing thing a new player hits is that order being violated. Still the only thing that gates shipping. |

> **Answered since the last edition**
>
> **The treasury rolled its whole debt in one bill** — a single six-month emergency note it repaid with money it did not have and wrote again, for ever. The note is retired: since 0.7.0 the central bank advances the gap at the policy rate, up to a ceiling the player sets, and past it the promises are paid and the rest owed. Term loans are issued at five benchmark maturities on a curve. The rest of that row — long bonds dominated past fifteen years, and rounded to $100M — was not re-measured; the rounding is at least stated on the borrow page now. **The overdraft had no floor** — a founding village given a university went to NaN by month 1,632 — and the advances ceiling is the floor. **The city borrowed below its own central bank's rate**, and the constant that did it is deleted. **The bank never paid for the city's paper**, and it does now. **Wages were indexed a third above the price level they chase** — closed without a fix, because it does not reproduce: `LabourCheck` holds the wage index to the published price index through 240 months of steady inflation, a reform and a reload, and on all eight seeds every one of 144 checkpoints sits at the level the two-year lag implies, wages over the index between 0.84 and 1.12. **The tuition table was calibrated against the wages before the rebalance**, and the price of a place is the player's dial now: at ×3 the trap the header describes is back, at ×1 it is quiet, and the balance call is at the player's hand.

> **Answered in the editions before**
>
> **Is the city too rich against its food?** — answered, and the answer was not the food. Measured against Canada the wholesale price was sane and the shops' markup was sane, but the *poorest* cell held about three times what an average Canadian does per head, and Jerus deferred the question until households carried transport and luxury costs, which they now do. The households looked rich against a basket with two things in it because they *were* rich, for a reason nothing on the page had measured: their savings abroad compounded at the world's 2% with the coupon rolled where it was earned, so net worth climbed to five thousand months of GDP and every household was past satiation on a shelf that was the only thing it could buy. The wealth term, the coupon paid home, cars, boutiques and kitchens gave the money somewhere to go, and the honest hunger measure then showed the shops delivering a fraction of what was asked — the food share was never the question; the supply wall is. **The transit loss** — $5.4M a month at the default fare, carried as a balance problem — was a ride charged once a month; forty journeys a month and it is gone. **The savings that cannot be spent** have their reading: the discharge tests the wage and never the savings. **The fare was collected from nobody**, and is a fee on every rider's statement now. **Nothing about transport was on a screen** — it is a tab with four pages.
>
> **Materials were priced nine times too low** — $18,000 a unit now, every template re-derived, and it found an import bill that had never been paid. **Retail's shelf price was the last unpriced half** — done; hunger sat at 0–1% and the shops delivered 94–96% of what they planned, on a hunger measure that was later found to be reading the shops' own denominator, so those two figures were never the city's (see the supply wall above). **Unemployment** — 12.8–15.5% at the end of eight seeds, against 41.5% when it was the largest open problem.
>
> **The two-hundred-year plateau** — answered by giving the city customers who do not live in it. A city whose every buyer is one of its own people can only grow as fast as it grows; with business services and manufacturing selling abroad, the median run went from 16,834 people with six seeds in sixteen ever taking off, to **127,651 with sixteen of sixteen**, and the price level from 0.799 to 0.975. **Nothing borrows below cost** — one rule closed the bond floor, the business desk and the carry trade at once. **The mills made food out of nothing** — they buy crops now, and the plant's return fell from 6.2% of build cost a month to about 3.9%.
>
> **A laid-off parent orphaned their children** — answered. The children of an adult who leaves work now go with them, at the city's own rate, and live on whatever that household lives on. Worst orphan month on the probe city **2,093.7 → 12.4**; child deaths over one 4,000-month seed **55,546 → 47,503**. **One good called Food fed everybody** — the shelf is thirteen foods, chosen by income, and the good called Food has been retired behind them. **A line that made two things was charged for both twice** — the sector cost methods divided a whole line's payroll, power and inputs by one good's output, which made an oven with two products produce nothing at all, and had been quietly over-costing business services and manufacturing since the day each shipped. Joint costs are split by relative sales value now, and a sector making one good is bit-for-bit what it was.

> **Judge nothing by a single playtest**
>
> Four thousand months of a chaotic trajectory diverge on the first differing decision. The same change measured +18% on one land seed and −28% on another, and a perturbation of one part in a million moves the long-run size of the city by 10%. Vary the seed, and measure the symptom rather than the end state.
